IPLA/Geometry.lean.title: Scaled coordinates for the parameter and particles
IPLA/Geometry.lean.summary:
Use orthogonal coordinates for the common parameter and the scaled latent particles. Their norm satisfies \(\|z\|^2=\|\theta\|^2+N^{-1}\sum_i\|x_i\|^2\). The average over physical particle energies is therefore the squared Euclidean norm of the latent blocks. This relation determines the particle factors in the convexity, gradient, and Euler-update formulas.

Fix a particle count \(N\), independent dimensions \(d_\theta,d_x\), and a joint potential \(U\). Write \(z=(\theta,z_1,\ldots,z_N)\), where the physical particles are \(x_i=\sqrt N z_i\). The lifted potential is \(V_N(z)=\sum_iU(\theta,\sqrt N z_i)\). This module derives its dimension, strong convexity, smoothness and exact Euler coordinates; none is an additional hypothesis.

steps.title: The coordinate spaces and their dimensions
steps.body:
A scaled particle state belongs to \(\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\times(\mathbb R^{d_x})^N\); a parameter–particle pair belongs to \(\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\times\mathbb R^{d_x}\). The parameter block and the latent blocks are mutually orthogonal, so their dimensions add:

\[\dim(\mathrm{State})=d_\theta+Nd_x,\qquad \dim(\mathrm{Joint})=d_\theta+d_x.\]

The block map returns \(z_i\), and its corresponding physical pair is \(A_i z=\operatorname{joint}_i(z)=(\theta,\sqrt N z_i)\). The potential \(V_N\) is the sum of the pair potentials at these physical coordinates. Thus \(\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\times(\mathbb R^{d_x})^N\) contains one common parameter and one scaled block for each particle. Changing the parameter changes every pair, whereas changing a single latent block changes only that pair. This distinction determines which gradient coordinates are summed and which acquire a factor of \(N\).

Formal correspondence: State : The scaled IPLA state: the common parameter followed by \(N\) particle blocks. Joint : A parameter-particle pair, with parameter block first. finrank_state : IPLA has one common parameter and \(N\) latent vectors, in arbitrary, independent parameter and latent dimensions. finrank_joint : The original joint potential has one parameter block and one latent block. block : Extract the scaled latent vector of particle \(i\). joint : Pair the common parameter with the unscaled \(i\)-th particle. potential : The potential used by ULA after scaling the particles by \(1/\sqrt N\).

steps.title: A sum of squared pair norms
steps.body:
The extraction map \(A_i\) is linear because its parameter and latent coordinates are linear functions of the state. In the sum of the extracted squared norms, each parameter coordinate occurs \(N\) times and each latent coordinate is multiplied once by \(\sqrt N\). Expanding the norms therefore gives

\[\sum_i\|A_i z\|^2=N\|\theta\|^2+N\sum_i\|z_i\|^2=N\|z\|^2.\]

The equality uses \((\sqrt N)^2=N\) and remains valid when \(N=0\), since both finite sums then have the required zero contributions. Linearity gives the corresponding identity for two states, \(\sum_i\|A_i(z-w)\|^2=N\|z-w\|^2\). Applying this sum of squares in the convexity and gradient estimates retains the precise particle factor; estimating the extraction maps separately would give a less precise bound.

Formal correspondence: joint_norm_sq_sum : Squared Euclidean norms of all replicated pairs sum to exactly \(N\) times the squared norm in scaled particle coordinates.

steps.title: Strong convexity of the summed pair potential
steps.body:
Assume that \(U\) is \(m\)-strongly convex. For weights \(a,b\ge0\) satisfying \(a+b=1\), its defining inequality at each pair is

\[U(aA_ix+bA_iy)\le aU(A_ix)+bU(A_iy)-\frac{mab}{2}\|A_i(x-y)\|^2.\]

Sum over \(i\). Linearity identifies the left-hand arguments with \(A_i(ax+by)\), and the squared-norm identity applied to \(x-y\) identifies the sum of quadratic terms. Consequently \(V_N\) is strongly convex with constant \(Nm\). The map \(A_i\) is continuous because it is linear between finite-dimensional spaces. If \(U\) is differentiable, the chain rule and the finite sum imply differentiability of the sum of \(U\circ A_i\).

More explicitly, the summed quadratic correction is \((mab/2)\sum_i\|A_i(x-y)\|^2\), which equals \((Nmab/2)\|x-y\|^2\). The curvature factor is therefore exactly \(N\) times the pair curvature. The argument includes weights zero and one, for which the correction vanishes, and requires no differentiability for the convexity conclusion.

Formal correspondence: potential_strongConvex : Strong convexity of the original pair potential gives \(Nm\) strong convexity of the scaled particle potential, with no extra hypothesis. jointCLM : The linear joint-pair extraction map. potential_differentiable : Differentiability survives the finite sum and the coordinate scaling.

steps.title: The gradient chain rule and the lifted Lipschitz constant
steps.body:
Assume that the pair potential is differentiable. In a direction \(w\), the chain rule gives

\[\langle abla V_N(z),w angle=\sum_i\langle abla U(A_i z),A_iw angle.\]

Cauchy–Schwarz in the particle index and the squared-norm identity give \(\sum_i\|A_iv\|\|A_iw\|\le N\|v\|\|w\|\). If \( abla U\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, subtraction of the directional formulas at two states yields

\[\langle abla V_N(x)- abla V_N(y),w angle\le NL\|x-y\|\|w\|.\]

Set \(w= abla V_N(x)- abla V_N(y)\). A zero gradient difference already satisfies the desired estimate; otherwise division by its positive norm shows that \( abla V_N\) is \(NL\)-Lipschitz. Applying the same argument to the absolute value gives \(|\langle abla V_N(x)- abla V_N(y),w angle|\le NL\|x-y\|\|w\|\), which is also the dual-norm form of the estimate. Both curvature and gradient regularity are multiplied by \(N\), so the condition number is \(L/m\) whenever the curvature is positive.

To track the constants without a coordinatewise overestimate, test the score difference against an arbitrary \(w\). The chain rule gives a sum of pair-gradient differences paired with \(A_iw\). Smoothness bounds it by \(L\sum_i\|A_i(x-y)\|\|A_iw\|\), and Cauchy–Schwarz over particles makes this \(NL\|x-y\|\|w\|\). Taking \(w\) equal to the score difference and cancelling its norm, with the zero case separate, proves the exact \(NL\) Lipschitz constant. This is the content of inner_gradient_potential, sum_joint_norm_mul and the final norm comparison.

Formal correspondence: inner_gradient_potential : Chain rule for the lifted potential, stated as an inner-product identity. sum_joint_norm_mul : Cauchy--Schwarz in the replicated pair coordinates. potential_gradient_lipschitz : Smoothness scales by \(N\), exactly as strong convexity does.

steps.title: The two gradient blocks
steps.body:
Let \(e_j\) be a parameter basis vector. Each \(A_i e_j\) is the corresponding parameter basis vector in the pair space. For the latent basis vector of particle \(i\), one has \(A_qe_{i,j}=0\) whenever \(q e i\), while \(A_i e_{i,j}=\sqrt N e_j\). Substitution in the directional derivative formula gives

\[ abla_ heta V_N(z)=\sum_i abla_ heta U( heta,\sqrt Nz_i),\qquad ( abla V_N(z))_i=\sqrt N abla_xU( heta,\sqrt Nz_i).\]

These are the two coordinate derivatives before multiplication by the step divided by \(N\). The parameter derivative of \(V_N\) contains every summand because the parameter is common to all pairs. For a latent block, the substitution \(x_i=\sqrt N z_i\) contributes a derivative factor \(\sqrt N\) to its single summand. Multiplication by \(\gamma/N\) then produces the parameter average and the physical-particle drift.

Formal correspondence: gradient_potential_parameter : The common parameter derivative is the sum of the pair derivatives. gradient_potential_particle : The scaled particle derivative is \(\sqrt N\) times the pair derivative.

steps.title: The parameter projection is a contraction
steps.body:
The parameter projection \(p_\theta z=\theta\) is linear and continuous. Orthogonality of the blocks gives \(\|p_\theta z\|^2\le\|z\|^2\) because every omitted squared coordinate is nonnegative. Taking square roots gives \(\|p_\theta z\|\le\|z\|\), and the definition of the operator norm gives \(\|p_\theta\|\le1\).

For two states, linearity also gives \(\|p_\theta z-p_\theta w\|\le\|z-w\|\). Applying this inequality to the two coordinates of a coupling shows that parameter projection cannot increase its quadratic cost. The inequality remains valid after taking an \(L^2\) norm. It therefore converts a full-state transport estimate into an estimate for the parameter, to which the equilibrium error about a deterministic center can then be added.

Formal correspondence: parameterCLM : Project the scaled state to its common parameter vector. norm_parameterCLM_apply_le : Forgetting the particle coordinates is a contraction. norm_parameterCLM_le_one : The parameter projection has operator norm at most one.

steps.title: Equivalence of the scaled and physical updates
steps.body:
For physical step \(h\), define the scaled Euler update by

\[z'=z- rac hN abla V_N(z)+\sqrt{2h/N}\,\xi.\]

The parameter coordinate is \( heta'= heta-(h/N)\sum_i abla_ heta U( heta,x_i)+\sqrt{2h/N}\,\xi_ heta\). Suppose \(N>0\). Multiplication of the \(i\)-th latent coordinate by \(\sqrt N\) gives drift coefficient \((\sqrt N)^2h/N=h\) and noise coefficient \(\sqrt N\sqrt{2h/N}=\sqrt{2h}\). Thus the physical latent update is

\[x_i'=x_i-h abla_xU( heta,x_i)+\sqrt{2h}\,\xi_i.\]

The factors arise from the pair derivatives: the latent derivative contains \(\sqrt N\), and conversion back to physical coordinates contributes another \(\sqrt N\). For step notation used in the probabilistic algorithm, \((\gamma/N)\sqrt N\sqrt N\) is therefore \(\gamma\) and the latent noise coefficient is \(\sqrt{2\gamma}\). The parameter noise coefficient remains \(\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\). Positivity of \(N\) justifies the divisions.

For \(\gamma>0\), the Gaussian parameter variance in each coordinate is \(2\gamma/N\), while each physical latent variance is \(2\gamma\). These are precisely the variances of the interacting particle updates. The coordinate equivalence is an equality of updates and does not involve a discretization approximation.

The square-root identity follows by multiplying radicands and cancelling positive \(N\); Lean's real square-root convention makes the algebraic identity valid for the stated arbitrary real \(h\) as well.

Formal correspondence: scaledUpdate : One IPLA step represented in the scaled joint coordinates. scaledUpdate_parameter : The common parameter update is exactly the average-gradient IPLA update. scaledUpdate_particle : Unscaling a particle coordinate gives its usual IPLA update, including the \(\sqrt{2h}\) noise coefficient.

IPLA/Model.lean.title: Statistical target, initialization and Gaussian innovations
IPLA/Model.lean.summary:
The statistical parameter maximizes the likelihood obtained by integrating out one latent variable. The sampling distribution is instead a Gibbs probability on the parameter and all particles. Its parameter marginal has density proportional to \(M^N\). Normalization and a change of latent coordinates establish this relation.

This file names the original parameter–latent statistical objects and the law of the actual algorithm. Definitions identify a density and a candidate maximizer; normalization, existence and concentration are proved in later modules.

steps.title: The marginal likelihood and its maximizer
steps.body:
Represent a parameter and latent vector by \(\operatorname{pair}(\theta,x)=(\theta,x)\) and define the marginal likelihood by

\[M(\theta)=\int_{\mathbb R^{d_x}}e^{-U(\theta,x)}\,dx.\]

The nonnegative extended integral defines this quantity before its finiteness is known. A maximizer \(\theta_*\) satisfies \(M(\theta)\le M(\theta_*)\) for every \(\theta\). When \(U=-\log p_\theta(x,y)\), this is the marginal-likelihood maximization problem. Including a parameter prior in \(U\) gives the maximum a posteriori problem.

This global definition does not require a derivative of the marginal likelihood. Once positivity and finiteness have been proved, maximization is equivalent to minimization of \(\Phi=-\log M\). Strong convexity of this negative log marginal then gives uniqueness, while continuity and coercivity give existence.

Formal correspondence: pair : The original parameter/latent pair \((\theta,x)\), parameter first. For fixed observations \(y\), the standard IPLA potential is \(U_y(\operatorname{pair}(\theta,x))=-\log p_\theta(x,y)\). The geometry and dynamics work with the fixed slice \(U_y\). marginalDensity : Unnormalized marginal density of the parameter, integrating out the latent variable. For \(U_y(\theta,x)=-\log p_\theta(x,y)\), this is the marginal likelihood \(p_\theta(y)\). A parameter prior may instead be included in \(U_y\). IsMarginalMaximizer : The parameter maximizes the integrated joint density. This is maximum likelihood in standard IPLA notation, and MAP when the parameter prior is included in \(U\). Its existence is not asserted by this definition. IsMarginalMAP : Compatibility name for the prior-inclusive formulation.

steps.title: The Gibbs target and the innovation assumptions
steps.body:
For the summed potential \(V_N\), define \(\Pi_N=Z_N^{-1}e^{-V_N}\,dz\) using \(Z_N=\int e^{-V_N}\,dz\). At the level of this definition, the integral and normalization may be extended-valued. The probability property follows later from the potential assumptions.

Assume that every scalar innovation \(\xi_{k,a}\) has distribution \(\mathcal N(0,1)\), that all these variables are mutually independent over coordinates and times, and that the entire noise sequence is independent of the initialization. Thus independence is imposed on the countable family \((k,a)\mapsto\xi_{k,a}\). Independence of \(Z_0\) from that family ensures that each step uses a standard Gaussian vector independent of all preceding inputs. Square integrability in \(L^2\) by itself would imply neither the Gaussian distribution nor this independence.

The target has unnormalized density \(e^{-\sum_i U(\theta,\sqrt N z_i)}\). Since all latent blocks occur with the same parameter, their Gibbs distribution generally has dependence. No independence among the target coordinates or among the interacting iterates is assumed. The independence hypotheses concern the innovations and the initialization.

Formal correspondence: gibbsTarget : The normalized density in (49), with \(U_N\) the actual lifted potential. The integral and scalar are extended-valued. gibbsTarget_isProbability derives positive finite normalization from the original joint strong convexity, before any conversion to real numbers. GaussianInnovations : The actual update noise is independent standard Gaussian in every coordinate and time, and independent of initialization. These are distributional hypotheses, not a claim to have constructed a random sequence.

steps.title: The law of the \(L^2\) recursion
steps.body:
Assume that the initial state and each innovation belong to \(L^2(P)\). Put \(h=\gamma/N\) and define the iterates and their laws by

\[Z_{k+1}=Z_k-h abla V_N(Z_k)+\sqrt{2h}\,\xi_k,\qquad ho_k=(Z_k)_\#P.\]

The gradient bound \(\| abla V_N(z)\|\le\| abla V_N(0)\|+NL\|z\|\) shows that the drift has at most linear growth. The triangle inequality therefore makes every successor square-integrable whenever the current state and innovation are square-integrable. Induction gives this property at every finite iteration. The measure \( ho_k\) is the distribution of that iterate; the equality with the coordinate recursion identifies all later moment and convergence estimates with the stated particle algorithm.

The Lipschitz estimate for \( abla V_N\) ensures the drift update stays in \(L^2\). The definition of laws is precisely this pushforward. The dynamics module proves that its representatives agree almost everywhere with the ordinary pointwise IPLA recursion, so the eventual theorem concerns this actual algorithm.

Formal correspondence: laws : The laws of the actual noise-driven IPLA recursion, in scaled coordinates. The coordinate identities in Geometry.lean show that this is precisely the usual average-gradient parameter step and ordinary particle Langevin steps.

IPLA/Dynamics.lean.title: Pointwise particle recursion and square-integrable realizations
IPLA/Dynamics.lean.summary:
A square-integrable random vector may be treated as an equivalence class modulo almost-sure equality or as a chosen measurable map. Starting from the same initialization and innovations, the two recursive definitions agree almost surely at every finite iteration. Their parameter and physical-particle coordinates, and hence their probability laws, consequently agree.

The formal convergence proof uses equivalence classes in \(L^2\). This module proves that their pushforward laws equal those of the displayed coordinate algorithm, including the exact square-root noise coefficients.

steps.title: The pair potential in physical coordinates
steps.body:
For each particle \(i\), the scaled pair extraction satisfies

\[A_i z=\operatorname{pair}(p_\theta z,\sqrt N\,\operatorname{block}_i z).\]

Substituting this identity into the summed potential gives

\[V_N(z)=\sum_iU\bigl(p_\theta z,\sqrt N\,\operatorname{block}_iz\bigr).\]

To verify the pair equality, compare the orthogonal coordinates. The parameter coordinate on each side is \(\theta\) and the latent coordinate is \(\sqrt N z_i\). The equality of potentials follows term by term in the finite sum. In particular every gradient evaluation in the physical recursion uses the original joint potential at the common parameter and the corresponding physical particle.

Formal correspondence: joint_eq_pair : A joint extraction is exactly the original parameter-particle pair after unscaling its particle. potential_eq_pair_sum : The lifted potential is the sum of the original pair potential, with physical particles equal to \(\sqrt N\) times the scaled particle blocks.

steps.title: The explicit recursion and its two block formulas
steps.body:
Given initialization \(Z_0=z_0\) and innovations, define \(Z_{k+1}=T_\gamma(Z_k,\xi_k)\). Applying the parameter and latent coordinate formulas to \(Z_k\) yields

\[\theta_{k+1}=\theta_k-\frac\gamma N\sum_i\nabla_\theta U(\theta_k,x_k^i)+\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\,\xi_k^\theta,\]\[x_{k+1}^i=x_k^i-\gamma\nabla_xU(\theta_k,x_k^i)+\sqrt{2\gamma}\,\xi_k^i,\qquad x_k^i=\sqrt N(Z_k)_i.\]

The latent-coordinate conversion requires \(N>0\) to cancel the factors of \(N\). All forces are evaluated at the preceding state: the parameter force is their average, and the force on each latent particle is its pair gradient. Both formulas use the coordinates of the same innovation vector. Thus the change between scaled and physical coordinates preserves each recursive step.

Formal correspondence: scaledChain : IPLA as an ordinary recursion on scaled states and noise vectors. scaledChain_parameter : The parameter recurrence in the pointwise IPLA chain. scaledChain_particle : The physical-particle recurrence in the pointwise IPLA chain.

steps.title: Equality of the square-integrable and pointwise recursions
steps.body:
The representative of the \(L^2\) initialization equals the pointwise initialization almost surely. Assume equality of the two iterates at time \(k\). The representative of the successor satisfies the Euler formula on a probability-one event. Intersecting this event with the preceding equality event and using \(2(\gamma/N)=2\gamma/N\) proves equality at time \(k+1\). Induction therefore gives

\[\rho_k=P\circ\bigl[\omega\mapsto Z_k^{\mathrm{pt}}(\omega)\bigr]^{-1}.\]

Each induction step intersects finitely many probability-one events, so no simultaneous choice over real times is required. For any measurable set \(A\), the two random vectors belong to \(A\) with the same probability. This equality of inverse-image probabilities proves equality of their pushforward laws.

The representative induction uses equality almost everywhere at each fixed finite time. In the successor case the intersection of the update's representative event and the previous induction event still has full measure, so substitution is legitimate. Once the random variables agree almost everywhere, Measure.map_congr gives equality of their laws. This step is what permits results proved for the Hilbert-space recursion to be presented as results for the explicit coordinate algorithm displayed above.

Formal correspondence: lpChain_coe : The \(L^2\) chain represents the explicit IPLA recursion almost everywhere. This includes the exact identity between \(\sqrt{2(\gamma/N)}\) and the noise coefficient \(\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\) in the displayed IPLA update. laws_eq_scaledChain : The laws appearing in the final theorem are exactly the laws of the explicit, noise-driven, pointwise IPLA recursion.

IPLA/AlgorithmLaw.lean.title: Gaussian innovation sequences and the laws of the iterates
IPLA/AlgorithmLaw.lean.summary: Mutual independence and the scalar standard Gaussian distributions determine the probability law of the entire innovation sequence. Independence of initialization makes their joint law a product measure. Applying the measurable finite-step recursion to this product proves that the output law depends only on the initial law, potential, and step, even when the random variables are defined on different probability spaces.

steps.title: A countable product of Gaussian innovations
steps.body:
Index scalar innovations by \((k,a)\), with the first index denoting time and the second a state coordinate. Define the countable product probability \(\bigotimes_{(k,a)}\mathcal N(0,1)\) on scalar sequences \(w\). The coordinate-grouping map is specified by \((\operatorname{pack}w)_k(a)=w(k,a)\). Each output coordinate is a measurable product projection, so the map to the vector-valued sequence is measurable.

A cylinder event restricts finitely many scalar coordinates. Its probability is the product of the corresponding Gaussian probabilities, and these cylinder probabilities determine the product measure uniquely. Taking the pushforward by the grouping map therefore gives standard Gaussian vectors with independent coordinates and independent time indices. The scalar product and its measurable pushforward both have total mass one.

The two probability instances are proved as well: each scalar Gaussian factor has mass one, hence the infinite product is a probability measure; pushing it through measurable packing preserves total mass. These are canonicalFlatNoiseLaw_isProbabilityMeasure and canonicalNoisePathLaw_isProbabilityMeasure, whose source appears in the complete-module panel.

Formal correspondence: NoiseCoordinate : A coordinate records the iteration and the parameter or particle block. canonicalFlatNoiseLaw : The canonical scalar noise source: independent standard real Gaussians. packNoisePath : Group scalar coordinates into the Euclidean noise vector at each time. packNoisePath_measurable : Packing the countable coordinate source is measurable. canonicalNoisePathLaw : The canonical vector-valued Gaussian noise-path law.

steps.title: Identification of the innovation-sequence distribution
steps.body:
Suppose the scalar innovations are mutually independent and each has distribution \(\mathcal N(0,1)\). The joint distribution of a countable independent family is the product of its coordinate distributions, giving

\[\mathcal L((\xi_{k,a})_{k,a})=\bigotimes_{k,a}\mathcal N(0,1).\]

Composition with the measurable coordinate-grouping map gives \(\mathcal L((\xi_k)_k)=\mathcal G\). Indeed independence identifies every finite-coordinate cylinder probability, and uniqueness of the countable product measure identifies the entire scalar-sequence law. The pushforward then identifies the vector-sequence law.

The conclusion specifies dependence across times as well as within each vector. Separate standard Gaussian distributions at each time would not suffice, since they would permit temporal dependence. It is the distribution of the full sequence that determines the repeated Gaussian transition.

Formal correspondence: GaussianInnovations.flatNoisePath_law : The Gaussian coordinate hypotheses identify the complete flattened path law. GaussianInnovations.noisePath_law : The vector-valued path law is derived from the scalar Gaussian hypotheses, including every coordinate and every iteration.

steps.title: Equality of the recursive update maps
steps.body:
The common update map is \(T(z,u)=z-(\gamma/N)\nabla V_N(z)+\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\,u\). Two recursions using this map, the same initialization, and the same innovations agree at time zero. If they agree at time \(k\), application of \(T\) with the same \(k\)-th innovation proves agreement at time \(k+1\). This induction is deterministic and requires no assumption about the distributions of its inputs.

The generic pointwise ULA update for \(V_N\) and step \(\gamma/N\) is \(z-(\gamma/N)\nabla V_N(z)+\sqrt{2(\gamma/N)}\xi\). Reassociating multiplication inside the square root makes it the scaled IPLA update. The generic noise-driven chain and scaledChain therefore agree by induction: their initial values match and each successor uses the same map on the same preceding state and noise vector.

Formal correspondence: pointwiseUpdate_eq_scaledUpdate : The generic ULA update for \(U_N\) is exactly the scaled IPLA update. noiseDrivenChain_eq_scaledChain : Exact identification of the generic noise recursion with the IPLA recursion.

steps.title: A common initial law gives common output laws
steps.body:
Let \(F_k(z_0,\xi)\) denote the measurable result of applying the update \(k\) times. If the initialization is independent of the Gaussian sequence, their joint law is \(\mu_0\otimes\mathcal G\), where \(\mathcal G\) is the sequence distribution above. The output law is therefore

\[\rho_k=(F_k)_\#(\mu_0\otimes\mathcal G).\]

Measurability follows by finite composition of the measurable update. Since the scaled particle update and the Gaussian Euler update coincide, the same pushforward describes the particle law at time \(k\). More explicitly, \(F_k\) depends only on the initial value and the first \(k\) innovations. Consequently any two realizations with the same initial law and independent Gaussian sequence have equal output laws, regardless of their underlying probability spaces. Auxiliary couplings may thus be chosen for the convergence argument while preserving the algorithm marginals.

The pointwise/\(L^2\) identity identifies this measure with laws. The right-hand side depends only on \(U,\gamma,\mu_0\), so two Gaussian realizations with the same initial law give identical output laws. This identity needs no stationary diffusion or reference coupling.

Formal correspondence: laws_eq_canonicalChainLaw : The law in the IPLA convergence statement is the canonical law of the actual Gaussian algorithm. No reference process is involved in this result. laws_eq_of_initialLaw_eq : Two Gaussian realizations of IPLA with the same initial law have the same output law, even when they use different underlying probability spaces.

IPLA/Foundations.lean.title: Normalization, moments and score moments of the lifted target
IPLA/Foundations.lean.summary: Gaussian domination of a strongly convex Gibbs density implies a finite positive partition function and finite second moments. The gradient regularity also bounds the equilibrium squared score. Apply these facts to \(V_N\), whose differentiability and \(Nm\)-strong convexity follow from the assumptions on \(U\). The resulting moments justify the transport and drift-integral estimates.

steps.title: Normalization and the second moment of the Gibbs target
steps.body:
The target is \(\Pi_N(dz)=Z_N^{-1}e^{-V_N(z)}\,dz\). Assume \(N>0\) and \(m>0\), so that \(Nm>0\). Differentiability and strong convexity imply a quadratic lower bound. Gaussian integrability then gives \(0

In detail, completing the affine part of the strong-convexity lower bound gives \(V_N(z)\ge a\|z\|^2-b\) with \(a>0\). The density is consequently at most \(e^b e^{-a\|z\|^2}\). Multiplication by \(\|z\|^2\) preserves integrability of this Gaussian majorant. The strictly positive exponential has positive integral under Euclidean volume, so \(Z_N>0\). Division by this positive finite integral proves both the probability property and the claimed second moment.

The geometry has already proved that \(V_N\) is differentiable and \(Nm\)-strongly convex. Its quadratic lower bound dominates \(e^{-V_N}\) and its norm-weighted powers by integrable Gaussian functions, giving a finite positive partition and finite second moment. The first declaration identifies the named target with the shared normalized Gibbs definition; the next two apply the normalization and moment theorems with modulus \(Nm>0\). Thus target mass one and finite moments are consequences of the original joint assumptions.

Formal correspondence: gibbsTarget_eq_gibbsMeasure : IPLA's target is exactly the general normalized Gibbs density. gibbsTarget_isProbability : Normalization of the lifted target follows from strong convexity of the original joint potential; no separate Gibbs normalization hypothesis. gibbsTarget_memLp : The lifted target has a finite second moment from the original joint strong-convexity assumption. Gradient Lipschitz continuity is not needed.

steps.title: Square integrability from finite quadratic transport
steps.body:
Let \(X\) be a measurable initialization satisfying \(W_2(X_\#P,\Pi_N)<\infty\). The Gibbs target has a finite second moment. Choose a coupling with finite quadratic cost and integrate \(\|x\|^2\le2\|x-y\|^2+2\|y\|^2\). Its first marginal gives the initial second moment, while its second marginal gives the target moment. Both terms on the right have finite integral, hence \(X\in L^2(P)\).

Finiteness of the Wasserstein distance guarantees a finite-cost coupling; attainment of the infimum is unnecessary. This argument permits finite initial transport distance to replace a separate initial second-moment assumption.

Formal correspondence: initial_memLp_of_finite_transport : An actual measurable initialization at finite \(W_2\) from the lifted Gibbs measure automatically belongs to \(L^2\). This justifies the \(L^2\) representation used by the main analytic theorem without an independent moment assumption.

steps.title: The lifted Gibbs score second moment
steps.body:
For a strongly convex potential with \(\ell\)-Lipschitz gradient, the Gibbs score estimate is \(\int\| abla V\|^2d\pi\le\ell\dim H\). The substitutions \(V=V_N\), \(\ell=NL\), and \(\dim H=d_ heta+Nd_x\) therefore give

\[\int\| abla V_N(z)\|^2d\Pi_N(z)\le NL(d_ heta+Nd_x).\]

The pair-potential assumptions imply all regularity hypotheses for this application. Since the gradient includes the parameter and every particle coordinate, its squared moment involves the full-state dimension. In the abbreviation \(NL D\), the dimension is \(D=d_ heta+Nd_x\). The later drift-integral estimate combines this moment with a step of length \(\gamma/N\). The parameter concentration estimate is a separate result and involves only the parameter dimension. No Hessian assumption or additional score-moment assumption is used.

Finite initial Wasserstein distance to a target with finite second moment implies finite initial second moment via a finite-cost coupling and \(\|X\|^2\le2\|X-Y\|^2+2\|Y\|^2\). The next theorem applies the shared Gibbs-score estimate to the actual lifted score with constant \(NL\), obtaining \[\mathbb E_{\Pi_N}\| abla V_N\|^2\le NL(d_ heta+Nd_x).\] The dimension substitution uses finrank_state; a separate Hessian or score-moment premise is unnecessary.

Formal correspondence: gibbsTarget_score_moment : The lifted Gibbs score moment also follows from the original joint potential assumptions; no separate score hypothesis or Hessian is introduced.

IPLA/Scaling.lean.title: Particle and time scaling of the transport estimate
IPLA/Scaling.lean.summary:
Substitution of the lifted curvature, gradient constant, dimension, and step into the Euclidean Langevin estimate gives the particle estimate. The dimension factor reduces to \(D/N=d_x+d_\theta/N\) because the scaled step is the physical step divided by the particle count. All substitutions below are equalities, so the numerical coefficient is preserved.

The lifted ULA problem has \(m_N=Nm\), \(L_N=NL\), step \(h=\gamma/N\), and dimension \(D=d_\theta+Nd_x\). This module performs the exact scalar substitutions into the shared Dalalyan theorem.

steps.title: Step restriction and square-root bias
steps.body:
Assume \(N>0\). Division by \(N\) preserves inequalities, and \(Nm+NL=N(m+L)\). Hence \(\gamma/N\le2/(Nm+NL)\) is equivalent to \(\gamma\le2/(m+L)\). The regularity ratio \(NL/(Nm)\) equals \(L/m\), while the dimension–step product satisfies

\[\frac\gamma N(d_\theta+Nd_x)=\gamma\left(d_x+\frac{d_\theta}{N}\right).\]

Nonnegativity of the dimensions and step permits the square-root product rule, giving

\[\frac{33}{20}\frac{NL}{Nm}\sqrt{\frac\gamma N D}=\frac{33}{20}\frac Lm\sqrt{d_x+d_\theta/N}\sqrt\gamma.\]

In terms of the lifted quantities \(m_N=Nm\), \(L_N=NL\), \(h=\gamma/N\), and \(D=d_\theta+Nd_x\), positivity of \(N\) gives \(L_N/m_N=L/m\) and

\[hD=\gamma(d_x+d_\theta/N).\]

The square-root identity is therefore \(\sqrt{hD}=\sqrt{d_x+d_\theta/N}\sqrt\gamma\). Every cancellation of \(N\) uses \(N>0\). The latent contribution is proportional to \(d_x\), whereas the parameter contribution is divided by \(N\). Thus particle count reduces the parameter contribution to discretization error; at a fixed physical step, the latent contribution persists. The admissible physical step does not depend on particle count.

Formal correspondence: scaled_step_iff : The original and rescaled step-size restrictions are equivalent. scaled_bias_eq : Exact equality of the Dalalyan discretization term with the term in (34).

steps.title: The transport estimate after scaling
steps.body:
Assume a family of comparison processes is available for every finite-cost initial coupling and that the initial \(W_2\) distance is finite. The Langevin transport theorem gives

\[W_2( u_k,\pi)\le(1-m_Nh)^kW_2( u_0,\pi)+ rac{33}{20} rac{L_N}{m_N}\sqrt{hD}.\]

The assumptions \(m\le L\), \(m>0\), \(\gamma>0\), and the physical step restriction imply the lifted hypotheses by multiplication and division by positive \(N\). The identity \(Nm(\gamma/N)=m\gamma\) simplifies the contraction, and the preceding square-root identity simplifies the dimension term. In particular \((1-m_Nh)^k=(1-m\gamma)^k\). The initial transport distance is already measured in the scaled state norm and acquires no additional particle factor. This proves the finite-time particle estimate under the stated comparison-process premise; the Gaussian construction establishes that premise for the algorithm laws.

The shared Hilbert-space theorem first gives \(W_2( u_k,\pi)\le(1-m_Nh)^kW_2( u_0,\pi)+(33/20)(L_N/m_N)\sqrt{hD}\). The local facts hNL and hs verify its compatibility and step premises from \(m\le L\) and the physical step restriction. Substituting \(m_Nh=m\gamma\) and the exact bias identity yields the displayed IPLA rate. This module expects an explicit stationary reference family; later modules construct that family before the public theorem invokes the estimate.

Formal correspondence: scaled_dalalyan : Dalalyan in the rescaled IPLA coordinates. Geometry will discharge the lifted convexity, differentiability and smoothness hypotheses from the joint potential. The only probabilistic inputs are the explicit reference family.

IPLA/ULAAdapter.lean.title: Equality with the Gaussian Euler transition laws
IPLA/ULAAdapter.lean.summary: The particle law equals the Gaussian Euler law for the summed potential and scaled step. Normalized Brownian increments provide the required independent innovations on a product probability space. Equality of the initialization and innovation-sequence laws then transfers this equality to any realization satisfying the algorithm assumptions. The construction of the stationary diffusion is used separately for the transport estimate.

steps.title: Gaussian innovations from Brownian increments
steps.body:
Let \(h=\gamma/N>0\). A scalar Brownian increment normalized as \([B_a((k+1)h)-B_a(kh)]/\sqrt h\) is centered Gaussian with variance one. Independence of increments on disjoint time intervals gives independence over \(k\), and independence of the scalar Brownian paths gives independence over \(a\). On the product probability space the Brownian sequence is also independent of initialization. These facts give mutual independence of all scalar innovation coordinates, standard Gaussian vector innovations, and independence of the next innovation from all preceding inputs.

On the independent product of an initial coupling and a Brownian source, define \(\xi_{k,a}=(B_a((k+1)h)-B_a(kh))/\sqrt h\). Each Brownian coordinate has centered Gaussian increments of variance \(h\), so each normalized coordinate has law \(\mathcal N(0,1)\). Independent Brownian coordinates and disjoint increments give mutual independence across coordinates and times. The product construction makes the complete noise path independent of the initial coupling. The shared product-noise theorems prove these three assertions, which are assembled into GaussianInnovations.

The local instance algorithmProductProbability follows because a coupling of probability measures has total mass one and the independent source law has mass one; their product therefore has total mass one. This justifies the probability-space hypotheses of the innovation and \(L^2\) law theorems.

Formal correspondence: productGaussianInnovations : The concrete product realization satisfies every distributional field of the actual IPLA algorithm. Standard Gaussian laws and all independence claims are conclusions from the independent Brownian coordinate source.

steps.title: The output law for a prescribed initial distribution
steps.body:
Suppose the auxiliary initial variable has law \(P\circ Z_0^{-1}\). The Brownian innovations satisfy the full Gaussian-sequence assumptions, so the law-uniqueness result identifies this recursion with any particle realization having the same initial law. In particular

\[\rho_k=\mu_0K_{\gamma/N}^{\,k}.\]

A finite-cost initial coupling and the target second moment make the auxiliary initial variable belong to \(L^2\). Although the joint auxiliary initial distribution depends on the chosen coupling, its first marginal remains \(\mu_0\). Independence makes the joint distribution of that first coordinate and the innovation sequence equal to \(\mu_0\otimes\mathcal G\). The output law is thus fixed as the coupling varies, as required when the convergence argument takes an infimum over initial coupling costs. No stationarity assertion is needed for this equality of laws.

Canonical Brownian Euler increments are proved standard Gaussian in every coordinate, mutually independent across times and coordinates, and independent of the coupled initialization. These are exactly the three fields of GaussianInnovations. Their initial law agrees with the supplied initialization law on the product extension, so canonical-law uniqueness identifies the resulting algorithm output laws. The final Markov-step identity then shows that the actual supplied chain iterates the same ULA kernel at step \(\gamma/N\).

Formal correspondence: laws_eq_productBrownianOutput : The law produced by the Brownian product construction is exactly the law of any supplied Gaussian IPLA realization with the same initialization. This bridge has no stationarity or reference-process hypothesis.

steps.title: Iteration of the Gaussian Euler kernel
steps.body:
For potential \(V_N\), step \(\gamma/N\), and gradient constant \(NL\), the grouped independent scalar innovations give the Gaussian Euler transition. Measurable representatives of the square-integrable recursion therefore satisfy

\[\rho_k=\mu_0K_{\gamma/N}^{\,k}.\]

The \(L^2\) representatives give the same laws as the pointwise iterates. To see the transition directly, denote the Euler kernel by \(K\). From a current law, the next law is \(\rho K\), the pushforward of \(\rho\otimes\mathcal N(0,I_D)\) through the update map. The next Gaussian vector is independent of the current state because the latter depends only on initialization and preceding innovations. Induction gives \(\rho_k=\mu_0K^k\). Consequently moment and transport estimates for this kernel apply to the particle recursion.

Formal correspondence: laws_eq_ulaLawStep : The actual IPLA law is precisely ULA for the rescaled lifted potential. All vector Gaussian and independence facts follow from the displayed scalar innovation specification of the algorithm.

IPLA/Generator.lean.title: Physical-time generator and Gibbs integration identity
IPLA/Generator.lean.summary: The continuous model in physical time is \(dZ_t=-N^{-1} abla V_N(Z_t)dt+\sqrt{2/N}\,dB_t\). Its generator is obtained by multiplying the usual lifted Langevin generator by the reciprocal particle count. For scaled state \(z\), a duration in physical time is \(N\) times the corresponding duration in lifted Langevin time, and the operator is \(N^{-1}(\Delta- abla V_N\cdot abla)\). Integration against the Gibbs density gives infinitesimal invariance; stationarity of the constructed evolution requires the separate diffusion argument.

steps.title: The physical-time generator on twice differentiable tests
steps.body:
Define \(\mathcal A_N\varphi=N^{-1}\mathcal L_{V_N}\varphi\), where \(\mathcal L_V\) is the Langevin generator of the summed potential. For a \(C^2\) test function, its coordinate expression is

\[\mathcal A_N\varphi(z)= rac1N\left(\Delta\varphi(z)-\langle abla V_N(z), abla\varphi(z) angle ight).\]

The diffusion has covariance rate \((2/N)I\), whose second-order generator term is \(\Delta/N\). The drift term is \(-\langle abla V_N, abla\varphi angle/N\). Their sum gives the displayed formula. Multiplication of the generator by a positive time constant changes the relaxation rate and preserves the Gibbs density determined by \(V_N\); the operator identity alone does not establish stationarity of a process.

Formal correspondence: diffusionGenerator : Generator in the physical IPLA time variable, acting on the rescaled state. diffusionGenerator_eq : The exact Laplacian and drift formula for the IPLA generator.

steps.title: Integration by parts and infinitesimal invariance
steps.body:
Let a compactly supported \(C^2\) function \(\varphi\) be given. Differentiability and gradient regularity of the joint potential imply the corresponding regularity of the lifted potential. Integration by parts proves that \(\mathcal L_{V_N}\varphi\) is integrable and has zero Gibbs integral. Multiplication by \(N^{-1}\) then gives

\[\int\mathcal A_N\varphi\,d\Pi_N= rac1N\int\mathcal L_{V_N}\varphi\,d\Pi_N=0.\]

Equivalently, a compactly supported \(C^2\) test satisfies \(\int[\Delta\varphi-\langle abla V_N, abla\varphi angle]d\Pi_N=0\). The physical generator has factor \(N^{-1}\). The integration-by-parts identity follows from

\( abla\!\cdot(e^{-V_N} abla\varphi)=e^{-V_N}(\Delta\varphi-\langle abla V_N, abla\varphi angle)\).

Compact support makes the boundary integral vanish and bounds all derivatives on the region of integration. Continuity of the score on that region ensures integrability. Division by the positive Gibbs partition and by \(N\) proves the normalized identity. Positive strong convexity also gives the probability property of the target. Thus the integral is a justified finite integral, rather than an expression assigned a default value when integrability fails. The passage to time-evolution stationarity is proved independently.

Formal correspondence: gibbsTarget_infinitesimalInvariant : Gibbs infinitesimal invariance for IPLA under only the original joint potential hypotheses. Integrability is a conclusion, so the zero integral cannot result from Lean's default value for a nonintegrable function.

IPLA/Degenerate.lean.title: Zero-dimensional parameter and state spaces
IPLA/Degenerate.lean.summary: A zero-dimensional Euclidean space consists of one vector. Consequently the parameter error vanishes when the parameter dimension is zero, and every probability law is the same point mass when the full state dimension is zero. These cases give the convergence inequality directly and allow the parameter and latent dimensions to be arbitrary nonnegative integers.

steps.title: Vanishing parameter error when \(d_\theta=0\)
steps.body:
Assume \(d_\theta=0\). The parameter space has one element, so \(p_\theta z=\theta_*\) for every state and every choice of center. Hence \(\|p_\theta z-\theta_*\|^2=0\) pointwise, and its integral and the square root of its integral are zero.

This conclusion does not require a probability measure or assumptions on the potential and noise. In particular it remains valid when the latent state has positive dimension: the sampling process may be nontrivial while the projected parameter error is identically zero.

Formal correspondence: parameterRMS_zero_dimension : There is no parameter error when the parameter dimension is zero. This holds for every latent dimension and every measure.

steps.title: The transport estimate on a singleton state space
steps.body:
Suppose the parameter dimension is zero and also \(d_x=0\). The state space is a singleton. Any two probability laws on it are the same point mass and have \(W_2\) distance zero: their coupling is concentrated on the diagonal and has zero cost. The equilibrium radius \(\sqrt{2d_\theta/(Nm)}\) and the discretization factor \(\sqrt{d_x+d_\theta/N}\) also vanish. Thus the asserted inequality reduces to \(0\le0\), independently of \(m,\gamma,L\).

The two degeneracies can be distinguished explicitly. Under \(d_\theta=0\) every parameter error vanishes, even if latent coordinates remain. Under the additional condition \(d_x=0\), all state-space transport distances vanish as well. The result follows without applying a positive-dimensional analytic estimate.

Formal correspondence: zero_dimensions_bound : The complete displayed error bound in the zero-dimensional state. No regularity of a potential, noise law, or initialization is needed here.

IPLA/MarginalConcentration.lean.title: The marginal likelihood and the parameter Gibbs distribution
IPLA/MarginalConcentration.lean.summary:
The joint strong-convexity assumptions imply that the latent-integrated likelihood is finite, positive, continuous, and tends to zero at parameter infinity. It therefore attains a maximum. Product integration and the particle-coordinate Jacobian identify the parameter marginal of the normalized particle Gibbs law with the normalized \(N\)-th power of that likelihood. The changes of variables contribute finite positive constants independent of the parameter, and these cancel upon normalization.

For differentiable jointly \(m\)-strongly convex \(U\), \(m>0\), this module proves finite positive latent partitions, continuity and vanishing parameter tails, existence of a maximizer, and the exact parameter projection of \(\Pi_N\). It establishes these facts before any logarithm, real conversion or concentration estimate is used.

steps.title: Orthogonal decomposition of the pair norm
steps.body:
The joint vector has parameter coordinates \(\theta_j\) and latent coordinates \(x_j\). Their orthogonal decomposition gives

\[\|\operatorname{pair}(\theta,x)\|^2=\|\theta\|^2+\|x\|^2.\]

The map \((\theta,x)\mapsto\operatorname{pair}(\theta,x)\) is continuous because each of its finitely many output coordinates is a continuous coordinate projection. It follows that continuous joint potentials have continuous parameter and latent slices. The norm identity also factors a Gaussian in the joint norm into a parameter Gaussian and a latent Gaussian. These facts justify the domination and continuity arguments for the latent integral.

Formal correspondence: norm_pair_sq : The pair coordinates preserve the orthogonal decomposition into parameter and latent variables. continuous_pair : Joint continuity of the parameter/latent pairing.

steps.title: A uniform Gaussian majorant for the latent integral
steps.body:
Assume positive strong convexity and differentiability. Bounding the affine term in the supporting quadratic at zero gives

\[U(v)\ge U(0)- rac{\| abla U(0)\|^2}{m}+ rac m4\|v\|^2.\]

Set \(C=\exp(\| abla U(0)\|^2/m-U(0))\) and \(a=m/4>0\). Orthogonality of the pair coordinates and exponentiation imply

\[e^{-U( heta,x)}\le Ce^{-a\| heta\|^2}e^{-a\|x\|^2}\le Ce^{-a\|x\|^2}.\]

The last function is integrable in the latent variable and independent of \( heta\). Indeed the norm decomposition is \(\|\operatorname{pair}( heta,x)\|^2=\| heta\|^2+\|x\|^2\); discarding the nonnegative parameter term leaves a Gaussian in \(x\) uniform over \( heta\). Continuity gives measurability, and Gaussian domination gives integrability of each slice. Strict positivity of the exponential then implies positivity of its integral.

The lower bound follows directly from \(U(v)\ge U(0)+\langle abla U(0),v angle+(m/2)\|v\|^2\) and Young’s inequality \(\langle abla U(0),v angle\ge-\| abla U(0)\|^2/m-(m/4)\|v\|^2\). Subtracting the latter quadratic loss from the strong-convexity term leaves a strictly positive quadratic coefficient. The finite Gaussian integral is valid also in dimension zero. No restriction to a bounded parameter neighborhood is required.

Formal correspondence: marginal_weight_gaussian_bound : A Gaussian domination uniform in both the parameter and latent variable. marginal_weight_uniform_bound : An integrable bound for every parameter slice, with no local parameter restriction. integrable_marginal_weight : Every latent partition is integrable from joint assumptions alone.

steps.title: Positivity, finiteness, and continuity of the marginal
steps.body:
Define \(M(\theta)=\int e^{-U(\theta,x)}dx\). The nonnegative slice integrand is integrable, so its extended integral equals the ordinary real integral \(M(\theta)\) and is finite. Strict positivity of the integrand under nonzero Euclidean volume gives \(M(\theta)>0\). For a sequence \(\theta_n\to\theta\), continuity of \(U\) gives pointwise convergence of the latent integrands. Their common integrable Gaussian majorant permits dominated convergence, proving continuity of \(M\).

In particular \(M(\theta)\) is positive without requiring a lower Gaussian bound: a positive continuous integrand has positive integral on a sufficiently small ball, with the dimension-zero case given by the one-point volume measure. The upper majorant proves finiteness. These positive finite values justify the real logarithm in the marginal potential.

Formal correspondence: marginalDensity_eq_ofReal_integral : The finite extended integral agrees with the ordinary real marginal. marginalDensity_ne_top : The parameter marginal is finite, excluding infinite-likelihood maximizers. marginalDensity_pos : Every parameter has strictly positive marginal density. continuous_marginal_integral : Continuity of the real-valued marginal follows by dominated convergence. continuous_marginalDensity : The actual extended-valued marginal is continuous as well.

steps.title: Existence of a marginal maximizer from Gaussian decay
steps.body:
Integrating the Gaussian majorant without discarding its parameter factor gives

\[0The multiplicative constant is independent of \(\theta\), and the bound tends to zero as \(\theta\) tends to infinity. Thus \(M(\theta)\to0\). Since \(M(0)>0\), values outside a sufficiently large ball are smaller than \(M(0)\). Continuity and compactness then give a global maximum inside the ball.

In abbreviated form the bound is \(M(\theta)\le C e^{-c\|\theta\|^2}\) with finite \(C\) and \(c>0\). Continuity of \(M\) and the tail limit \(M(\theta)\to0\) as \(\|\theta\|\to\infty\) imply attainment because \(M\) is positive at a fixed parameter. Quantitatively, choose \(R\) so that the upper bound is less than \(M(0)/2\) whenever \(\|\theta\|>R\). The maximum on the closed ball of radius \(R\) is at least \(M(0)\) and exceeds all values outside. This proves existence without differentiating the marginal. Uniqueness follows later from strong convexity of its negative logarithm.

Formal correspondence: marginal_integral_gaussian_bound : Joint strong convexity gives a Gaussian parameter tail after integrating out the latent variable. The constant is finite and independent of \(\theta\). tendsto_marginal_integral_cocompact : The parameter marginal vanishes at infinity. exists_marginalMaximizer : Existence of the actual marginal maximizer is derived from the original joint assumptions. No maximizer or compactness premise is introduced.

steps.title: Product integration and the dilation determinant
steps.body:
For nonnegative measurable functions, induction over \(n\) using Tonelli’s theorem gives

\[\int\prod_{i=1}^nf(x_i)\,d\mu^{\otimes n}=\left(\int f\,d\mu\right)^n.\]

The empty product has integral one; separating the last coordinate proves the induction step. The formula holds as an extended integral even before finiteness is known. For a nonzero dilation \(r\) in dimension \(d\), change of variables gives \(\int f(rx)dx=|r^d|^{-1}\int f(x)dx\). Applying this with \(r=\sqrt N\) under \(N>0\) yields

\[\int\prod_i e^{-U(\theta,\sqrt N z_i)}\,dz_1\cdots dz_N=\left(N^{-d_x/2}M(\theta)\right)^N.\]

For fixed \(\theta\), the exponential of the summed potential is \(\prod_i e^{-U(\theta,\sqrt N z_i)}\). In each block the substitution \(x_i=\sqrt N z_i\) contributes the inverse determinant \(N^{-d_x/2}\). The full latent integral is therefore \(N^{-Nd_x/2}M(\theta)^N\). This factor is finite and positive under \(N>0\) and independent of \(\theta\).

The determinant of dilation by \(\sqrt N\) in one block is \(N^{d_x/2}\); the integral uses its reciprocal. Repeating the change in \(N\) blocks gives the displayed common factor. Since every slice integral has already been shown positive and finite, the extended product identity can then be read as an ordinary finite identity.

Formal correspondence: lintegral_fin_prod_eq_pow : Tonelli factorization of identical nonnegative weights over finitely many independent latent coordinates. This extended-integral statement also records divergence correctly; no integrability premise is hidden. lintegral_comp_smul_eq : Change of variables for a nonnegative weight under scalar dilation. scaled_particle_partition : Integrating the actual scaled particle potential at a fixed parameter gives the \(N\)-th power of the original marginal, times the explicit scalar Jacobian. This is the factor that cancels in the normalized parameter law.

steps.title: A linear equivalence with parameter–particle product coordinates
steps.body:
Define \(C(\theta,(z_i)_i)\) by inserting the parameter coordinates followed by all latent blocks. Its inverse is \(z\mapsto(p_\theta z,(\operatorname{block}_iz)_i)\). Coordinatewise evaluation proves the inverse identities and linearity, so both directions are continuous in finite dimension. In particular \(p_\theta C(\theta,z)=\theta\) and \(A_iC(\theta,z)=\operatorname{pair}(\theta,\sqrt N z_i)\).

Thus grouping the coordinates gives a linear bijection of the full state spaces. The potential in product coordinates is evaluated at the same parameter and physical particles. Product integration and density projection may consequently be performed in these coordinates, with the associated volume factor accounted for separately.

Formal correspondence: configuration : Assemble the scaled state from its parameter and particle blocks. configurationCLE : Grouping coordinates is a constructed continuous linear equivalence.

steps.title: The density of the projected unnormalized measure
steps.body:
The finite sum defining \(V_N\) gives the exponential factorization

\[e^{-V_N(C(\theta,z))}=\prod_i e^{-U(\theta,\sqrt N z_i)}.\]

Two measure identities justify integration in the grouped coordinates. For a measurable equivalence \(e\), the pushforward of \(\mu\) with density \(w\circ e\) under \(e\) is \((e_\#\mu)\) with density \(w\). This follows by integration over an arbitrary measurable set. Moreover the first-coordinate projection of \(w(\theta,z)d\mu(\theta)d\nu(z)\) has density \(\int w(\theta,z)d\nu(z)\) with respect to \(\mu\), by Tonelli’s theorem.

For a measurable parameter set \(A\), this projection identity integrates \(\mathbf 1_A(\theta)e^{-V_N(\theta,z)}\) over both coordinate groups. Integrating the latent coordinates first gives a function of \(\theta\), and integrating that function over \(A\) gives the projected measure of the set. Equality for every measurable \(A\) identifies the measures. Substitution of the exponential factorization then gives the explicit fiber density.

Formal correspondence: weight_configuration : In grouped coordinates the actual Gibbs weight factors over particles. map_withDensity_comp_equiv : A density commutes with a measurable coordinate equivalence. map_fst_withDensity : Tonelli's theorem identifies the first-coordinate density of a weighted product measure.

steps.title: Cancellation of positive finite normalization constants
steps.body:
A continuous linear equivalence takes Euclidean volume to a Haar measure. The resulting measure is \(c\) times the target volume, where \(c\) is finite and positive. For a measure \(\mu\) satisfying \(0<\mu(E)<\infty\) and a scalar satisfying \(0\[\frac{c\mu}{(c\mu)(E)}=\frac{\mu}{\mu(E)}.\]

The identity follows because scalar multiplication also multiplies the total mass. The positive finite mass of \(\mu\) makes both normalized measures probability measures. Both the grouping factor and the latent dilation factor are independent of \(\theta\). Replacing the measure by \(c\mu\) changes its mass to \(c\mu(E)\), and positivity and finiteness of \(c\) permit cancellation. Therefore neither change of variables changes the normalized parameter distribution.

Formal correspondence: normalize_smul_eq : Normalization is unchanged by multiplication by any finite positive constant. This is why grouping coordinates and the particle Jacobian cancel. configuration_map_volume : The finite-dimensional coordinate grouping changes volume by a constructed finite positive constant. Its value is irrelevant after normalization.

steps.title: The parameter marginal of the normalized Gibbs distribution
steps.body:
Define \(\pi_N^\theta(d\theta)=Z_\theta^{-1}M(\theta)^N d\theta\). For the unnormalized measures \(\mu=e^{-V_N}dz\) and \(\rho=M(\theta)^Nd\theta\), grouping the coordinates introduces the volume scalar \(c\), while latent integration introduces \(J^N\) with \(J=N^{-d_x/2}\). The density pushforward calculation gives \(c\,p_{\theta\#}\mu=J^N\rho\). These constants are finite and positive, so normalization and preservation of total mass under projection imply

\[p_{\theta\#}\Pi_N=\pi_N^\theta.\]

After integration, the parameter density is proportional to \(M(\theta)^N\); all other factors are independent of \(\theta\). Consequently the normalized identity is

\[(p_\theta)_\#\Pi_N(d\theta)=\frac{M(\theta)^N\,d\theta}{\int M(u)^Ndu}.\]

In terms of the total latent factor \(J=N^{-Nd_x/2}\), the unnormalized density is a fixed coordinate-volume multiple of \(J M(\theta)^N\). The same multiple appears in its partition and cancels. Since \(M\) is positive, raising it to the positive integer \(N\) preserves comparisons. Hence the parameter mode is a maximizer of the original marginal likelihood. The probability and finite-moment properties also follow from the projection identity.

Formal correspondence: marginalTarget : The parameter law with density proportional to the \(N\)-th power of the original latent marginal. This names the statistical target without assuming anything about its concentration.

steps.title: The marginal partition and second moment
steps.body:
The projection of the probability \(\Pi_N\) is \(\pi_N^\theta\), so the latter has mass one. Its unnormalized density \(M^N\) is positive, hence its partition is positive. An infinite partition would make the defined normalized density zero and contradict mass one; the partition is therefore finite.

The projection \(p_\theta\) is bounded and linear. Applying the pushforward integral formula to the finite lifted second moment gives \(\theta\mapsto\theta\in L^2(\pi_N^\theta)\). More explicitly, \(\|p_\theta z\|^2\le\|z\|^2\) bounds the projected squared norm by the full squared norm. This establishes a finite marginal second moment before a numerical concentration estimate is applied.

Formal correspondence: marginalTarget_isProbability : The marginal power density normalizes to a probability measure as a consequence of its proved equality with the actual Gibbs projection. marginalPartition_pos : The normalizer of the powered marginal density is strictly positive. marginalPartition_ne_top : The powered marginal partition is finite. Its proof uses the previously established probability identity, so divergence cannot disappear in a real conversion or an infinite normalizing constant. marginalTarget_memLp : The parameter marginal has finite second moment, without a separate marginal moment or concentration assumption.

IPLA/PrekopaLeindler.lean.title: One-dimensional Prékopa–Leindler inequality
IPLA/PrekopaLeindler.lean.summary: Let the two one-dimensional densities be continuous, strictly positive, and have finite positive integrals. Their cumulative distribution functions define an increasing transport map. Its derivative, together with the weighted arithmetic–geometric mean inequality and change of variables, proves the normalized Prékopa–Leindler inequality. Rescaling the densities proves the inequality for arbitrary finite positive masses.

steps.title: Differentiability and strict increase of the cumulative integral
steps.body:
Let \(f\) be continuous, strictly positive, and integrable on \(\mathbb R\), with \(\int f=1\). Its cumulative distribution function is \(F(x)=\int_{(-\infty,x]}f\). Splitting the integral at zero gives

\[F(y)-F(0)=\int_0^y f(t)dt\]

The fundamental theorem of calculus gives \(F'(x)=f(x)\). Thus the cumulative function is differentiable and continuous. For \(y>x\), the difference \(F(y)-F(x)=\int_x^y f(t)dt\) is positive because a positive continuous function has positive integral on a nonempty interval. Consequently the cumulative function is strictly increasing. The infinite lower limit is constant in the local differentiation argument.

Formal correspondence: Density : A positive, continuous probability density on the real line. cumulative : Cumulative integral of an ordinary real density.

steps.title: The cumulative range and the open unit interval
steps.body:
Integrability gives \(F(x)\to0\) as \(x\to-\infty\). Splitting the unit integral at \(x\) gives \(F(x)=1-\int_{(x,\infty)}f\), hence \(F(x)\to1\) as \(x\to+\infty\). Positivity first gives \(0\le F\le1\). Strict monotonicity, applied at \(x\) and its neighboring points \(x-1\) and \(x+1\), then gives \(0

For any \(u\in(0,1)\), the endpoint limits supply two finite arguments whose cumulative values lie below and above \(u\). Continuity gives an argument with \(F(x)=u\), and strict monotonicity makes it unique. Therefore \(F(\mathbb R)=(0,1)\). The inverse cumulative function is consequently defined exactly on the open unit interval; neither endpoint is attained at a finite argument.

steps.title: The increasing transport map and its derivative
steps.body:
For cumulative distribution functions \(F,G\), define \(T=G^{-1}\circ F\). Both have range \((0,1)\), so \(G(T(x))=F(x)\). Strict monotonicity makes \(G\) injective, and \(G'(T(x))=g(T(x))>0\) permits the inverse-function theorem. The chain rule gives

\[T'(x)=\frac{f(x)}{g(T(x))}>0.\]

In particular \(T\) is strictly increasing. The identity \(G(T(x))=F(x)\) equates the cumulative probabilities at corresponding arguments. Its differentiated form is \(g(T(x))T'(x)=f(x)\). The denominator is positive, so division is justified and yields the derivative and density change-of-variables relation. Both the map and its derivative follow from the density assumptions.

For positive continuous unit-mass densities, \(F(x)=\int_{-\infty}^xf\) and \(G(y)=\int_{-\infty}^yg\) are differentiable with strictly positive derivatives, hence strictly increasing, and their limits give range \((0,1)\). Define \(T=G^{-1}\circ F\), so \(G(T(x))=F(x)\). The inverse-function derivative gives \(T'(x)=f(x)/g(T(x))>0\). The cumulative identities and strict monotonicity declarations justify this change of variables on the whole real line.

Formal correspondence: transport : The monotone transport from density \(f\) to density \(g\).

steps.title: Change of variables in the normalized inequality
steps.body:
Assume \(0\le t\le1\) and the interpolation inequality \(h((1-t)x+ty)\ge f(x)^{1-t}g(y)^t\). Define \(S(x)=(1-t)x+tT(x)\) and \(r=f(x)/g(T(x))>0\). The derivative is \(S'=1-t+tr>0\). Weighted arithmetic–geometric mean gives \(r^t\le1-t+tr=S'\). Applying the interpolation inequality with \(y=T(x)\) therefore yields

\[f(x)=f(x)^{1-t}g(T(x))^t r^t\le h(S(x))S'(x).\]

The increasing map \(S\) permits change of variables. Its right-hand integral becomes the integral of \(h\) over \(S(\mathbb R)\), which is at most the integral over \(\mathbb R\) by nonnegativity. Since the first density has mass one, \(1\le\int h\). The extended nonnegative integral makes this valid without assuming integrability or continuity of \(h\).

The cancellation can also be written directly in terms of \(S(x)=(1-t)x+tT(x)\). The hypothesis gives a lower bound on \(h(S(x))\) by \(f(x)^{1-t}g(T(x))^t\); the derivative satisfies \(S'(x)=(1-t)+tT'(x)\ge T'(x)^t\). Since \(T'=f/g(T)\), multiplication gives \(h(S(x))S'(x)\ge f(x)\) and integration gives \(\int h\ge\int f=1\). For nonunit masses, divide \(f,g\) by their positive integrals; restoration of their normalizations gives the factor \((\int f)^{1-t}(\int g)^t\).

The scalar inequality \((1-t)+tr\ge r^t\) is valid for all \(r>0\) and includes \(t=0,1\). Substituting \(r=f/g(T)\) is the reason the density factors cancel after multiplication by the Jacobian. The argument integrates only over the image of the interpolating map; nonnegativity of \(h\) makes surjectivity unnecessary.

Formal correspondence: normalized_prekopa_leindler : The normalized one-dimensional Prékopa--Leindler inequality, proved by the constructed monotone transport. The third weight need not be continuous or integrable; the conclusion is an extended nonnegative integral.

steps.title: The inequality for arbitrary positive finite masses
steps.body:
A strictly positive integrable function on a nonzero measure space has positive integral. Write \(A=\int f>0\), \(B=\int g>0\), and \(C=A^{1-t}B^t>0\). Apply the normalized result to \(f/A\), \(g/B\), and \(h/C\). The identity \(\log(f/A)=\log f-\log A\) verifies the rescaled interpolation inequality. If \(h\) is also nonnegative and integrable, the extended conclusion becomes \(1\le(\int h)/C\). Multiplication by \(C\) gives

\[\exp\!\left((1-t)\log\int f+t\log\int g\right)\le\int h.\]

Thus normalization of \(f\) and \(g\) changes the interpolation factor by \(A^{1-t}B^t\), and multiplication by that positive finite factor recovers the original statement. The logarithms occur only at positive numbers and therefore also define the formula at endpoint weights. The positivity argument applies to the one-point measure in dimension zero as well.

Formal correspondence: integral_positive : Strict positivity of the real integral of an everywhere positive integrable function, including the zero-dimensional product space used in tensorization. prekopa_leindler_real : Prékopa--Leindler on the real line for arbitrary positive continuous integrable first and second weights. No normalization is assumed.

IPLA/PrekopaTensorization.lean.title: Finite-dimensional Prékopa–Leindler with Gaussian tails
IPLA/PrekopaTensorization.lean.summary: To prove Prékopa–Leindler in finite dimension, integrate one coordinate and apply induction to the remaining coordinates. Continuous strictly positive functions with Gaussian upper bounds remain in the same class after this integration. Gaussian domination proves the slice integrability, marginal continuity, positive marginal values, and marginal Gaussian bound required at every induction step.

steps.title: Integrability and positivity under Gaussian domination
steps.body:
In coordinates \(\mathrm{Coordinates}(n)=\mathbb R^n\), assume continuity, strict positivity, and \(f(x)\le Ce^{-a\sum_i x_i^2}\) with \(C,a>0\). The product of one-dimensional Gaussian integrals is finite, so domination gives \(f\in L^1\). Strict positivity under nonzero Euclidean volume gives \(\int f>0\). Multiplication by \(c>0\) preserves these properties and changes the upper-bound constant to \(cC\).

The coefficient \(a>0\) gives integrable Gaussian decay on \(\mathbb R^n\). Since the dominated function is positive, the bound also proves absolute integrability. These conclusions include the one-point space in dimension zero and permit the positive scalar factors introduced by convexity inequalities.

Formal correspondence: GaussianWeight : The class of positive continuous weights with a Gaussian upper bound.

steps.title: Continuity and integrability of slices and marginals
steps.body:
The coordinate insertion \((s,x)\mapsto(s,x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) is continuous. Define the first marginal by \(f_1(x)=\int_\mathbb R f(s,x)ds\). The identity \(\sum_i(s,x)_i^2=s^2+\sum_i x_i^2\ge s^2\) bounds every slice by \(Ce^{-as^2}\), independently of \(x\). Each slice is measurable by continuity and integrable by this Gaussian bound. If \(x_j\to x\), continuity gives pointwise convergence for every \(s\); dominated convergence then proves continuity of \(f_1\).

In \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\), write the inserted point as \(\operatorname{cons}(z,x)\) with integrated coordinate \(z\in\mathbb R\). For constants \(C,a>0\) the bound is explicitly

\[0<f(\operatorname{cons}(z,x))\le C\exp\!\left[-a\left(z^2+\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i^2\right)\right]\le C e^{-az^2}.\]

The same majorant applies to every value of the remaining coordinates. Each positive slice has positive finite integral. Thus the marginal is positive, finite, and continuous, as required for the lower-dimensional argument.

The last inequality drops a nonnegative sum of squares, so the majorant is independent of \(x\). It is integrable in \(z\) by the one-dimensional Gaussian integral theorem. The declaration slice_integrable uses positivity to identify the absolute value of the slice with the slice itself, continuity to obtain measurability, and this majorant to prove integrability.

Now let \(x_m\to x\). For every fixed \(z\), continuity of \(f\) and of coordinate insertion gives \(f(\operatorname{cons}(z,x_m))\to f(\operatorname{cons}(z,x))\). The same Gaussian majorant controls every term and the limit. Dominated convergence therefore gives convergence of their real integrals, proving continuity of the first marginal. In the Lean invocation of continuous_of_dominated, the four obligations are slice measurability, the uniform almost-everywhere bound, integrability of that bound, and pointwise continuity in the remaining coordinates. Those are all established before the induction later treats the marginal as another Gaussian weight.

Formal correspondence: continuous_cons : Continuity of inserting the first real coordinate. firstMarginal : Integrate out the first coordinate of a weight.

steps.title: Gaussian decay and the marginal total integral
steps.body:
Retaining the Gaussian decay in the remaining coordinates gives

\[f_1(x)\le C\left(\int_\mathbb R e^{-as^2}ds\right)e^{-a\sum_i x_i^2}.\]

The Gaussian integral in the coefficient is finite and positive. Positivity of each slice gives positivity of \(f_1\); together with continuity, this shows that \(f_1\) satisfies the same hypotheses as the original function. The coordinate decomposition preserves product volume, and Fubini’s theorem gives \(\int f_1=\int f\) because Gaussian domination has established absolute integrability.

The new upper-bound constant is the original constant multiplied by \(\int e^{-as^2}ds\), while the decay coefficient \(a\) is unchanged. Hence the argument can be repeated one coordinate at a time without adding analytic assumptions.

steps.title: Induction over the dimension
steps.body:
When \(n=0\), the space has one point and volume one, so the desired integral inequality is the given pointwise inequality. In dimension \(n+1\), fix the remaining-coordinate vectors \(x,y\). Apply the one-dimensional theorem to \(s\mapsto f(s,x)\), \(r\mapsto g(r,y)\), and \(u\mapsto h(u,(1-t)x+ty)\). Their integrals are the marginals \(f_1,g_1,h_1\), and the conclusion is precisely their pointwise interpolation inequality. Each marginal satisfies the Gaussian hypotheses, so the induction hypothesis in dimension \(n\) gives

\[\left(\int f\right)^{1-t}\left(\int g\right)^t\le\int h.\]

Positive powers may be written using exponentials and logarithms; this also includes \(t=0\) and \(t=1\). In the equivalent notation that splits \(\mathbb R^{d+1}\) into one coordinate and \(d\) others, the first application integrates the distinguished coordinate and leaves the interpolation inequality in \(d\) dimensions. Fubini identifies each resulting iterated integral with the original total integral. This proves the induction step and therefore the finite-dimensional theorem.

Formal correspondence: prekopa_leindler : The finite-dimensional Prékopa--Leindler inequality. The induction uses the proved real-line transport theorem and integrates one coordinate at a time.

IPLA/StrongLogConcavity.lean.title: Strong convexity of the negative log marginal likelihood
IPLA/StrongLogConcavity.lean.summary: Joint strong convexity gives a parameter quadratic term in the pointwise interpolation inequality. Applying Prékopa–Leindler to the latent variables retains this term, so \(-\log M\) is strongly convex. More precisely, define \(M(\theta)=\int e^{-U(\theta,x)}dx\) and \(\Phi(\theta)=-\log M(\theta)\). The positive finite marginal and the finite-dimensional integral inequality show that \(\Phi\) has curvature \(m\). This also proves uniqueness of the marginal-likelihood maximizer.

steps.title: Definition and minimizing points of the marginal potential
steps.body:
The latent integral \(M\) is positive, finite, and continuous. Therefore \(\Phi=-\log M\) is real-valued and continuous, since the logarithm is continuous away from zero. If \(\theta_*\) maximizes the extended marginal likelihood, its finite real representation gives \(\Phi(\theta_*)\le\Phi(\theta)\) for every \(\theta\) by monotonicity of the logarithm and negation.

The condition \(0
