Positivity and finiteness were proved from the joint assumptions in MarginalConcentration.lean . marginalPotential : The actual marginal negative log-likelihood, with the observations fixed. marginalMaximizer_minimizes_potential : The statistical marginal maximizer minimizes the actual negative log-likelihood. All real conversions use proved positive finite partitions.

steps.title: Gaussian-dominated weights in product coordinates
steps.body:
Let \(f_\theta(x)=e^{-U(\theta,x)}\) in ordinary latent product coordinates. The Gaussian bound gives \(f_\theta(x)\le Ce^{-m\|x\|^2/4}\); continuity and strict positivity therefore put each slice in the class required by Prékopa–Leindler. The Euclidean coordinate identification preserves volume, so its integral is \(M(\theta)\). Pairing respects differences and affine combinations:

\[\operatorname{pair}(\theta,x)-\operatorname{pair}(\theta',y)=\operatorname{pair}(\theta-\theta',x-y),\]\[\operatorname{pair}(a\theta+b\theta',ax+by)=a\operatorname{pair}(\theta,x)+b\operatorname{pair}(\theta',y).\]

Consequently the joint strong-convexity inequality can be applied to \((\theta,x)\) and \((\theta',y)\). Their squared distance separates into parameter and latent terms. Discarding only the nonnegative latent term retains the full parameter curvature in the integral inequality.

Formal correspondence: latentWeight : A latent slice written in ordinary product coordinates for applying the finite-dimensional Prékopa--Leindler theorem.

steps.title: Prékopa–Leindler with the parameter quadratic term
steps.body:
Take \(a,b\ge0\) with \(a+b=1\), and set \(\theta_r=a\theta+b\theta'\) and \(c=(mab/2)\|\theta-\theta'\|^2\). Strong convexity of \(U\) and the orthogonal pair norm imply

\[aU(\theta,x)+bU(\theta',y)\ge U(\theta_r,ax+by)+c,\]

Here the additional term \((mab/2)\|x-y\|^2\) has been discarded because it is nonnegative. Exponentiation gives the Prékopa premise with third weight \(e^{-c}f_{\theta_r}\), which is a positive constant multiple of a Gaussian-dominated slice. The integral inequality yields \(M(\theta)^aM(\theta')^b\le e^{-c}M(\theta_r)\). Positivity permits logarithms and negation, giving

\[\Phi(a\theta+b\theta')\le a\Phi(\theta)+b\Phi(\theta')-\frac{mab}{2}\|\theta-\theta'\|^2.\]

For the alternative parameter notation \(\theta_r=a\theta+b\vartheta\) under \(a+b=1\), the same pointwise step is

\[U(\theta_r,ax+by)\le aU(\theta,x)+bU(\vartheta,y)-\tfrac{mab}{2}\|\theta-\vartheta\|^2,\]

The multiplier is \(e^{-c}\) with \(c=mab\|\theta-\vartheta\|^2/2\). Thus its integral conclusion is \(M(\theta)^aM(\vartheta)^b\le e^{-c}M(\theta_r)\). In the first notation, setting \(c=(mab/2)\|\theta-\theta'\|^2\) gives the exponential inequality \(e^{-c}e^{-U(\theta_r,ax+by)}\ge e^{-aU(\theta,x)}e^{-bU(\theta',y)}\), whose Prékopa conclusion is \(e^{-c}M(\theta_r)\ge M(\theta)^aM(\theta')^b\). Taking logarithms gives \(\log M(\theta_r)\ge a\log M(\theta)+b\log M(\theta')+c\). Negation proves strong convexity with modulus \(m\) and the stated quadratic coefficient \(1/2\). All latent integrals are positive and finite, so every transformation is a real-valued one.

Every marginal integral is already finite and positive, so logarithms preserve the inequality. Negating gives \(F(\theta_r)\le aF(\theta)+bF(\vartheta)-c\), exactly \(m\)-strong convexity of \(F=-\log M\). The code's hpoint is the weight inequality, hpl its Prékopa integral consequence, and hlog its logarithmic conversion. Strict convexity for \(m>0\) then proves uniqueness of the previously constructed maximizer.

Formal correspondence: marginalPotential_strongConvex : Integrating out the latent variables preserves precisely the original strong-convexity constant. This is the derived Prékopa theorem for IPLA.

steps.title: Existence and uniqueness of the marginal maximizer
steps.body:
Assume \(m>0\). The established \(m\)-strong convexity makes \(\Phi\) strictly convex. Two marginal-likelihood maximizers would both minimize \(\Phi\). If they were distinct, the midpoint inequality would contradict minimality. Existence has already followed from continuity and decay of the marginal, so there is \(\exists!\theta_*\) satisfying the original maximization condition.

Specifically, the midpoint value would be at most the common minimum minus \((m/8)\|\theta-\theta'\|^2\). This subtraction is strictly positive for distinct parameters because \(m>0\). The contradiction proves uniqueness without requiring a derivative of the marginal potential.

Formal correspondence: marginalMaximizer_unique : Joint strong convexity implies uniqueness of the marginal maximizer. existsUnique_marginalMaximizer : The marginal maximizer exists uniquely under exactly the original joint potential assumptions.

IPLA/Concentration.lean.title: Equilibrium concentration of the parameter marginal
IPLA/Concentration.lean.summary: The parameter Gibbs potential is \(N\Phi\). Since its curvature is proportional to particle count, the continuous strongly convex Gibbs concentration inequality gives a parameter second moment inversely proportional to that count. The exact density is proportional to \(M(\theta)^N=e^{-N\Phi(\theta)}\); its potential has curvature \(Nm\) in dimension \(d_\theta\). The resulting equilibrium root mean square radius is \(\sqrt{2d_\theta/(Nm)}\). This is the available concentration estimate with factor two, derived without a separate concentration assumption.

steps.title: The scaled marginal potential and its Gibbs measure
steps.body:
Multiply the strong-convexity inequality for \(\Phi\) by \(N\). The affine terms and quadratic term are all multiplied by \(N\). Thus \(N\Phi\) has strong-convexity constant \(Nm\). Since \(M>0\), the exponential identity is

\[e^{-N\Phi(\theta)}=e^{N\log M(\theta)}=M(\theta)^N.\]

The equality \(e^{-N\Phi}=M^N\) holds at every parameter because \(M\) is positive and finite. The unnormalized measures therefore coincide, as do their normalized measures. The Gibbs concentration theorem can consequently be applied to the parameter target with curvature \(Nm\).

The finite-real representation of the original extended marginal identifies this weight exactly with the one defining marginalTarget. Its normalized law is therefore the shared Gibbs measure of \(N\Phi\).

Formal correspondence: scaled_marginalPotential_strongConvex : Multiplying the actual marginal potential by \(N\) multiplies its proved strong-convexity constant by \(N\). marginalTarget_eq_gibbsMeasure : The normalized powered marginal density is exactly the Gibbs law of the proved \(N\)-scaled negative log marginal.

steps.title: The parameter second-moment estimate
steps.body:
A marginal-likelihood maximizer \(\theta_*\) minimizes \(\Phi\) and therefore \(N\Phi\). The continuous-potential Gibbs estimate applies without requiring differentiability of \(\Phi\) and yields

\[\int\|\theta-\theta_*\|^2d\pi_N^\theta(\theta)\le\frac{2d_\theta}{Nm}.\]

Its assumptions hold for \(N\Phi\) by continuity, the proved \(Nm\)-strong convexity, and the minimizing-point property. This estimate has factor two and needs only these assumptions. The dimension is \(d_\theta\) because the latent variables have already been integrated out. Their dimension does not enter this equilibrium parameter moment.

Formal correspondence: marginalTarget_secondMoment_le : Exact finite second-moment bound about any parameter maximizing the actual latent marginal. Its existence and uniqueness were proved separately.

steps.title: The projected moment under the lifted Gibbs law
steps.body:
The projection equality \(p_{\theta\#}\Pi_N=\pi_N^\theta\) and the pushforward integral formula give

\[\int\|p_\theta z-\theta_*\|^2d\Pi_N(z)\le\frac{2d_\theta}{Nm}.\]

The projected variable belongs to \(L^2\), and subtracting \(\theta_*\) preserves square integrability. The right-hand moment bound is nonnegative, so taking square roots gives

\[\operatorname{RMS}_{\Pi_N}(p_\theta-\theta_*)\le\sqrt{2d_\theta/(Nm)}.\]

For clarity, apply the pushforward identity to \(g(\theta)=\|\theta-\theta_*\|^2\). It states \(\int g(p_\theta z)d\Pi_N=\int g(\theta)d\pi_N^\theta\) and thus transfers the same moment estimate to the full-state Gibbs law without bounding latent deviations. Minkowski’s inequality can then add this equilibrium radius to a full-state coupling error. Joint differentiability and positive strong convexity suffice; the gradient-Lipschitz assumption is not used in this concentration step.

Powering the marginal density by \(N\) multiplies its negative log potential by \(N\), so its modulus becomes \(Nm\). The actual marginal maximizer minimizes that potential. The dilation concentration theorem used in this module bounds its parameter second moment by \(2d_\theta/(Nm)\), and the exact parameter pushforward identity gives the same moment under the lifted Gibbs law. The final square-root estimate uses the proved finite second moment to interpret projected \(L^2\) error as an ordinary integral. The stronger \(d_\theta/(Nm)\) constant is separately proved in the proximal sharp-concentration extension.

Formal correspondence: gibbsTarget_parameter_secondMoment_le : Transfer the proved marginal moment bound to the actual scaled IPLA Gibbs measure using the exact parameter-marginal identity. gibbsTarget_parameter_concentration : The equilibrium concentration input in IPLA Theorem 1 is a proved theorem of the original joint assumptions. No gradient-Lipschitz or marginal assumption is needed for this statistical term.

IPLA/Theorem.lean.title: The strongly convex IPLA parameter-error bound
IPLA/Theorem.lean.summary: The parameter error is bounded by equilibrium concentration, the remaining initial transport error, and the discretization error. For the observed-data potential \(U_y\), assume differentiability, \(m\)-strong convexity with \(m>0\), an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, \(N>0\), and \(0<\gamma\le2/(m+L)\). Assume square-integrable initialization and mutually independent standard Gaussian innovation coordinates, independent of initialization. Let \(\theta_*\) maximize the latent-integrated likelihood. The bound below holds for arbitrary nonnegative parameter and latent dimensions.

steps.title: The transport and equilibrium contributions to parameter error
steps.body:
Suppose the state dimension is positive. The summed potential has curvature \(Nm\) and gradient constant \(NL\) in dimension \(D=d_\theta+Nd_x\). Its Gibbs law \(\Pi_N\) is a probability with finite second moment, so square-integrable initialization gives finite initial quadratic transport. Apply Gaussian ULA with \(h=\gamma/N\). The scaled step restriction and the exact law identity give

\[W_2(\rho_k,\Pi_N)\le(1-m\gamma)^kW_2(\mu_0,\Pi_N)+\frac{33}{20}\frac Lm\sqrt{d_x+d_\theta/N}\sqrt\gamma.\]

The estimate is for a finite transport distance between the algorithm law and the Gibbs law. The equilibrium bound is \(\operatorname{RMS}_{\Pi_N}(p_\theta-\theta_*)\le\sqrt{2d_\theta/(Nm)}\). For any coupling of \(\rho_k\) and \(\Pi_N\), the projection norm bound \(\|p_\theta\|\le1\) and Minkowski’s inequality bound the parameter error by the coupling cost plus that equilibrium radius. Taking the infimum over couplings yields

\[\left(\int\|p_\theta z-\theta_*\|^2d\rho_k\right)^{1/2}\le\sqrt{\frac{2d_\theta}{Nm}}+(1-m\gamma)^kW_2(\mu_0,\Pi_N)+\frac{33}{20}\frac Lm\sqrt{d_x+\frac{d_\theta}{N}}\sqrt\gamma.\]

The moment assumptions needed in this argument follow from the joint potential hypotheses and \(L^2\) initialization. The substitutions in the Gaussian theorem are step \(\gamma/N\), curvature \(Nm\), gradient constant \(NL\), and dimension \(d_\theta+Nd_x\). For a coupling \((X,Y)\) with marginals \(\rho_k,\Pi_N\), the projection inequality used above is exactly \(\|p_\theta X-\theta_*\|_2\le\|X-Y\|_2+\|p_\theta Y-\theta_*\|_2\). Thus transport, concentration, and projection give the three displayed terms. Stationarity of the reference diffusion and the target concentration are derived results, rather than extra assumptions of this theorem.

The projection inequality gives \(R_{\theta_*}(\rho_k)\le W_2(\rho_k,\Pi_N)+R_{\theta_*}(\Pi_N)\); equilibrium concentration supplies the second term. The facts houtput and hmoment ensure finite values before projected RMS is rewritten as a square-root integral. Finally, the exact particle/time scaling simplifies the transport terms. Thus normalization, stationary reference and parameter concentration are derived inputs, while joint strong convexity, smoothness and the Gaussian innovation laws remain the stated assumptions.

Formal correspondence: nonempty_dimension_bound : For fixed observations \(y\), write \(U_y(\operatorname{pair}(\theta,x))=-\log p_\theta(x,y)\). The general-dimension counterpart of equation (34), with independent parameter dimension \(d_\theta\) and latent dimension \(d_x\), for the actual Gaussian IPLA recursion and its defined Gibbs target. Every hypothesis is displayed here or is one of the Gaussian-law and independence fields of GaussianInnovations , whose definition is included in the standalone file. Normalization, all finite transport moments, a stationary Langevin reference, and the equilibrium parameter concentration are derived in the proof.

steps.title: The zero-dimensional cases
steps.body:
Under \(N>0\), a positive parameter dimension supplies a parameter coordinate, and a positive latent dimension supplies a coordinate in a nonempty particle block. Hence the full state has no coordinates exactly when both dimensions are zero. Every other case is covered by the positive-state-dimension argument. In the remaining singleton case the parameter error, transport distance, and dimension-dependent error terms are all zero, so the same bound holds directly.

The public theorem splits on whether the state coordinate index type is nonempty. In the nonempty case, instantiate the preceding theorem directly, retaining arbitrary independent \(d_\theta,d_x\). If the index type is empty, its parameter part forces \(d_\theta=0\); since \(N>0\), a positive \(d_x\) would supply a latent coordinate, so \(d_x=0\) as well. Normalize the Gibbs target by the same strong-convexity theorem and apply the singleton-state bound, where every error, transport distance and dimension term vanishes. This completes the displayed estimate in all dimensions. Existence and uniqueness of a permissible \(\theta_*\) are established separately by existsUnique_marginalMaximizer, so the maximizer binder does not demand an unproved existence assumption.

Formal correspondence: theorem1 : Strongly convex IPLA for independent, arbitrary parameter and latent dimensions. All stationary-reference and concentration inputs are derived. The zero-dimensional cases are included without extra assumptions.

IPLA/LSI/Scaling.lean.title: Scaling of joint and per-particle entropy estimates
IPLA/LSI/Scaling.lean.summary: Let \(\beta\) be the logarithmic Sobolev constant of the lifted Gibbs target. Substitute \(h=\gamma/N\), \(\ell=NL\), and \(D=d_\theta+Nd_x\) into the Gaussian Euler entropy estimate. The full entropy and the entropy divided by particle count have different forcing and limiting error terms; both are computed below. The specialization \(\beta=N\alpha\) requires that constant for the lifted target itself.

steps.title: The lifted step and compatibility inequalities
steps.body:
Assume \(N>0\) and \(L>0\). Factoring the denominator and cancelling positive \(N\) gives

\[\frac\gamma N\le\frac\beta{4(NL)^2}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\gamma\le\frac\beta{4NL^2}.\]

If \(\beta=N\alpha\), cancellation of positive \(N\) also gives \(N\alpha\le NL\Longleftrightarrow\alpha\le L\) and \(N\alpha/(4NL^2)=\alpha/(4L^2)\). These are numerical equivalences; they do not prove a logarithmic Sobolev inequality.

The lifted theorem uses \(h=\gamma/N\), \(L_N=NL\), \(D=d_\theta+Nd_x\), and target constant \(\beta\). Its restriction \(h\le\beta/(4L_N^2)\) is therefore \(\gamma\le\beta/(4NL^2)\). Under the additional assumption \(\beta=N\alpha\) it becomes \(\gamma\le\alpha/(4L^2)\). Positivity of \(N\) justifies these steps.

Squaring the lifted gradient constant introduces \(N^2\). The scaled Euler step contributes \(1/N\), leaving one factor \(N\) in the physical restriction. Growth of the lifted logarithmic Sobolev constant proportional to \(N\) cancels that factor. Since the pair potentials share a parameter, this growth is not inferred from product tensorization of independent pair targets.

Formal correspondence: lifted_lsi_step_iff : The ULA restriction for the lifted step is exactly this IPLA restriction. linear_lsi_compatibility_iff : The scaled compatibility condition is equivalent to the base comparison. linear_lsi_step_iff : When the actual lifted LSI constant is \(N\alpha\), the IPLA step restriction has no remaining particle-number factor.

steps.title: The contraction exponent under time scaling
steps.body:
The identity \(-\beta(\gamma/N)k=-\beta\gamma k/N\) gives equality of the corresponding exponentials. If \(\beta=N\alpha\) and \(N>0\), the rate further satisfies

\[e^{-\beta\gamma k/N}=e^{-\alpha\gamma k},\qquad e^{-(N\alpha)(\gamma/N)k}=e^{-\alpha\gamma k}.\]

Thus uniformity in \(N\) requires the stated linear scaling of the lifted constant. In one step the exponent is \(\beta h\), and after \(k\) steps it is \(\beta hk\). The elapsed physical time is \(k\gamma\), so the decay coefficient per unit physical time is \(\beta/N\). A lower bound of order \(N\) on the lifted constant therefore gives a rate uniform in particle count.

Formal correspondence: lifted_entropy_rate_eq : The general decay rate retains the actual lifted LSI constant. linear_entropy_rate_eq : The rewritten general rate simplifies under the additional linear LSI scaling assumption. linear_ula_entropy_rate_eq : The same simplification directly from the ULA step notation.

steps.title: Full and per-particle entropy error terms
steps.body:
The Gaussian Euler entropy estimate has error term \(8hD\ell^2/\beta\). Substitution of the lifted quantities gives

\[\frac{8(\gamma/N)D(NL)^2}{\beta}=\frac{8\gamma ND L^2}{\beta},\qquad \frac1N\frac{8\gamma ND L^2}{\beta}=\frac{8\gamma DL^2}{\beta}.\]

The dimension satisfies \(D/N=d_x+d_\theta/N\). Under \(\beta=N\alpha\), the per-particle error term is therefore

\[\frac{8\gamma DL^2}{N\alpha}=\frac{8\gamma L^2}{\alpha}\left(d_x+\frac{d_\theta}{N}\right).\]

The algebraic identity can treat \(\alpha=0\) separately, but entropy applications use \(\alpha>0\). Given \(H\le qH_0+8\gamma ND L^2/\beta\), divide the entire inequality by positive \(N\), including its initial term. The full error term \(8hDL_N^2/\beta=8\gamma NDL^2/\beta\) is divided by \(N\). Under \(\beta=N\alpha\) this gives \((8\gamma L^2/\alpha)(d_x+d_\theta/N)\), and the initial entropy is divided by \(N\).

The forcing in one step is instead \(6h^2DL_N^2=6\gamma^2DL^2\), whose normalized version is \(6\gamma^2L^2(d_x+d_\theta/N)\). This distinction accounts for the factor \(N\) between full and per-particle quantities. Division by \(N\) leaves the exponential unchanged. The error also depends on the full dimension \(D\); rewriting \(D/N\) displays the parameter and latent contributions separately.

Formal correspondence: lifted_entropy_bias_eq : The unnormalized entropy bias after substituting the lifted step and smoothness. The dimension \(D\) is kept as a scalar parameter. normalized_entropy_bias_eq : Dividing the entropy by the particle number cancels one bias factor. normalized_dimension_eq : The intensive dimension appearing in normalized entropy. linear_normalized_entropy_bias_eq : The normalized bias under an LSI constant \(N\alpha\) for the actual lift. normalize_entropy_bound : A general entropy bound can be divided by the positive particle number, with its initial contribution and bias both normalized exactly.

steps.title: Normalization of the one-step entropy recurrence
steps.body:
The scaled squared step and squared gradient constant satisfy

\[6(\gamma/N)^2D(NL)^2=6\gamma^2DL^2.\]

After division by \(N\), the dimension identity gives \(6\gamma^2DL^2/N=6\gamma^2L^2(d_x+d_\theta/N)\). Therefore the lifted one-step recurrence implies

\[\frac{H_{k+1}}N\le e^{-\beta\gamma/N}\frac{H_k}N+\frac{6\gamma^2DL^2}{N}.\]

The implication follows by division by positive \(N\) and substitution in the exponential and forcing. With \(\beta=N\alpha\), the ratio becomes \(e^{-\alpha\gamma}\) and the forcing becomes \(6\gamma^2L^2(d_x+d_\theta/N)\). This calculation assumes the recurrence; the interpolation theorem proves it for the Euler laws.

IPLA/LSI/Theorem.lean.title: Entropy convergence under interpolation regularity assumptions
IPLA/LSI/Theorem.lean.summary:
Assume a logarithmic Sobolev inequality for the lifted Gibbs target and regularity of the frozen-drift Gaussian interpolation. In this conditional result the density representation, weak equation, differentiability, and required integrability are explicit assumptions. They imply finite joint entropy, a one-step dissipative inequality, and the finite-time geometric estimate for the particle laws. Equality of the Gaussian Euler and particle laws transfers the conclusion to the given realization.

Let \(V_N(z)=\sum_iU(\theta,\sqrt Nz_i)\), \(D=d_\theta+Nd_x\), and \(\Pi_N\propto e^{-V_N}\). Assume differentiability and \(L\)-Lipschitz joint gradient, an LSI of constant \(\beta>0\) for this actual target, \(\beta\le NL\), and \(0<\gamma\le\beta/(4NL^2)\). Take an initial probability law \(\mu_0\). The endpoint also assumes RegularInterpolationData for \((V_N,\beta,\gamma/N,NL,\mu_0)\). These density, weak-equation, energy and moment obligations remain conditional; they have not been constructed from LSI and smoothness alone.

steps.title: Probability laws of the Gaussian particle recursion
steps.body:
The Gaussian Euler transition is the measurable pushforward of the product of a current probability law and an independent standard Gaussian law. It is therefore a probability kernel, and each finite iterate has total mass one. Independence of the innovation sequence identifies these iterated laws with the particle recursion. This identification does not require a stationary reference process.

Define \(\rho_k=\mu_0K_{\gamma/N}^{\,k}\); at \(k=0\) this is \(\mu_0\) by the iterate definition. The lifted gradient is \(NL\)-Lipschitz, so the measurable Gaussian transition preserves probability, and induction through the shared ULA law theorem proves \(\rho_k\) is a probability for every \(k\). If \(\mu_0\) is the initial law of the explicit independent-Gaussian IPLA recursion, laws_eq_ulaLawStep identifies it with this same iterate. Thus the entropy result concerns the actual algorithm rather than a substituted reference process.

Formal correspondence: particleLaws : The canonical Markov laws of IPLA, using its proved lifted-ULA transition. particleLaws_isProbability : The actual lifted IPLA transition preserves probability mass. particleLaws_eq_laws : These Markov laws agree with the existing noise-driven Gaussian IPLA realization, including its scalar coordinate laws and independence.

steps.title: Finiteness of the discrete joint entropy
steps.body:
The logarithmic Sobolev hypothesis includes normalization of \(\Pi_N\). Assume positive relative densities \(r_k(t)\) such that \(r_k(t)\Pi_N\) is the frozen-drift interpolation law, together with the stated spatial smoothness and local entropy regularity. At step \(h=\gamma/N\ge0\) the entropy-finiteness theorem gives

\[\operatorname{KL}(\rho_k\Vert\Pi_N)<\infty\quad\text{for every }k.\]

For a relative density \(r\), the entropy equals \(\int r\log r\,d\Pi_N\) when the integrand is integrable. The interpolation assumptions justify this integral and identify its interval endpoints with the discrete laws. In particular the entropy of \(\rho_k\) is finite. This conclusion is required before using the divergence as a real number in the differential inequality and recurrence.

The time-zero interpolation identity transfers this density-level KL finiteness to the actual iterate. In the probability-law application, the integrable entropy density also equals that actual finite KL. This guard precedes every use of toReal; infinite divergence is never turned into an artificial zero. The proof requires the supplied regularity, not a strong-convexity premise.

Formal correspondence: particle_kl_finite : The identified regular interpolation gives finite actual IPLA relative entropy. Target normalization follows from the lifted LSI assumption.

steps.title: The entropy differential inequality and one-step recurrence
steps.body:
Set \(h=\gamma/N\), \(\ell=NL\), and \(H_k=\operatorname{KL}(\rho_k\Vert\Pi_N)\). Assume the interpolation weak equation and the differentiation and integrability properties needed to test it with the logarithmic relative density. For the drift discrepancy \(e_k(t)\), the interpolation data give

\[\int r_k(t)\|e_k(t)\|^2d\Pi_N\le t^2\ell^2G_k+2tD\ell^2,\qquad G_k\le\frac{4\ell^2}{\beta}H_k+2D\ell.\]

Young’s inequality in the entropy derivative gives \(H'(t)\le-3J(t)/4+\int r\|e\|^2d\Pi_N\), and the logarithmic Sobolev inequality gives \(J(t)\ge2\beta H(t)\). Under \(h\le\beta/(4\ell^2)\) and \(\beta\le\ell\) one has \(h\ell\le1/4\) and \(\beta h\le1/4\). The drift-error estimates then yield

\[H'(t)\le-\frac32\beta H(t)+\frac\beta4H_k+\frac52hD\ell^2.\]

An affine differential comparison and \(e^{-3x/2}+x/4\le e^{-x}\) for \(0\le x\le1/4\) imply \(H_{k+1}\le e^{-\beta h}H_k+6h^2D\ell^2\). For the lifted model, positivity of \(L\) follows from \(0<\beta\le NL\). The scaled step and forcing identities therefore give

\[H_{k+1}\le e^{-\beta\gamma/N}H_k+6\gamma^2DL^2.\]

Division by positive \(N\) gives the normalized recurrence with forcing \(6\gamma^2L^2(d_x+d_\theta/N)\). The error field is the difference between the current-gradient drift and the drift frozen at the beginning of the interval. Young’s inequality absorbs its score pairing into Fisher dissipation, and the logarithmic Sobolev inequality bounds entropy by that dissipation. The step restriction limits the old-entropy contribution from the error so that the remaining recurrence is contractive. Thus the recurrence is derived from the regularity and error assumptions, rather than included among them.

Let \(H_k=\operatorname{KL}(\rho_k\Vert\Pi_N)\). The canonical laws are those of the actual lifted Gaussian Euler kernel, and the law identity relates them to the supplied realization. The regular interpolation data connect the density at both endpoints of every Euler interval to these same laws, and supply the analytic weak-equation and moment regularity used by the shared entropy theorem. Finite KL is proved before toReal is used.

Apply that theorem with \(h=\gamma/N\), \(L_N=NL\), dimension \(D\), and actual lifted LSI constant \(\beta\). The compatibility and positive-step facts are established by hL, hLs, hβLs and hscaled. The result is \[H_{k+1}\le e^{-\beta\gamma/N}H_k+6\gamma^2DL^2.\] The normalized declaration divides this proved inequality by positive \(N\) and substitutes \(D/N=d_x+d_\theta/N\).

Formal correspondence: particle_kl_one_step : The one-step entropy recurrence is derived from the regular weak interpolation equation. The forcing is \(6\gamma^2DL^2\) in the full state. particle_kl_one_step_normalized : The actual one-step recurrence per particle has the intensive dimension \(d_x+d_\theta/N\).

steps.title: Summation of the entropy recurrence
steps.body:
Let \(q=e^{-\beta h}\). Induction in the one-step inequality gives

\[H_k\le q^kH_0+6h^2D\ell^2\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}q^j.\]

Because \(0<\beta h\le1/4\), the estimate \(1-e^{-\beta h}\ge3\beta h/4\) bounds the geometric sum by \(4/(3\beta h)\). Consequently \(H_k\le e^{-\beta hk}H_0+8hD\ell^2/\beta\). Substituting \(h=\gamma/N\), \(\ell=NL\), and \(D=d_\theta+Nd_x\) yields

\[H_k\le e^{-\beta\gamma k/N}H_0+\frac{8\gamma ND L^2}{\beta}.\]

Divide every term by positive \(N\) to obtain

\[\frac{H_k}{N}\le e^{-\beta\gamma k/N}\frac{H_0}{N}+\frac{8\gamma DL^2}{\beta}.\]

The exponent controlling the geometric sum is \(\beta h\). The resulting full estimate is

\[H_k\le e^{-\beta\gamma k/N}H_0+\frac{8\gamma NDL^2}{\beta}.\]

Division by \(N\) applies to both the initial entropy and the error term. If the additional lifted-target assumption \(\operatorname{LSI}(\Pi_N,N\alpha)\) holds, substitution gives rate \(e^{-\alpha\gamma k}\) and dimension factor \(d_x+d_\theta/N\). The denominator of the geometric series is positive because \(\beta,h>0\). Its lower bound on \(1-e^{-\beta h}\) changes the quadratic one-step forcing to the linear-step error term. The finite sum is bounded in this way for every finite \(k\); no infinite-time limit is used.

Formal correspondence: particle_kl_bound : The shared ULA entropy argument in IPLA coordinates. The LSI constant \(\beta\) belongs to the full lifted target; in particular it is not assumed to equal \(N\) times a pair-target constant. particle_kl_bound_normalized : Dividing the full-state relative entropy by the particle number gives its natural per-particle normalization.

steps.title: Linear scaling of the lifted logarithmic Sobolev constant
steps.body:
Assume the lifted target has logarithmic Sobolev constant \(N\alpha\), with \(0<\alpha\le L\) and \(0<\gamma\le\alpha/(4L^2)\). Then \(N\alpha>0\) and \(N\alpha\le NL\), so the general conditional theorem applies after the step equivalence. Its exponential becomes \(e^{-\alpha\gamma k}\), and \(D/N=d_x+d_\theta/N\) gives

\[\frac{H_k}{N}\le e^{-\alpha\gamma k}\frac{H_0}{N}+\frac{8\gamma L^2}{\alpha}\left(d_x+\frac{d_\theta}{N}\right).\]

The substitution \(\beta=N\alpha\) is a hypothesis concerning the coupled lifted Gibbs law. After division by \(N\), its dimension term is \(d_x+d_\theta/N\). The common parameter prevents a product decomposition into independent parameter–particle targets. Accordingly a one-pair logarithmic Sobolev inequality alone does not supply this specialization.

Formal correspondence: particle_kl_bound_of_linear_lsi : If the lifted target actually has LSI constant \(N\alpha\), the rate is independent of \(N\) and the normalized dimension is \(d_x+d_\theta/N\). This is a specialization of a supplied lifted-target LSI, rather than a tensorization assertion about the original pair model.

steps.title: Equality of entropy estimates across Gaussian realizations
steps.body:
On probability space \(P\), assume square-integrable initialization and all the stated Gaussian coordinate and independence hypotheses. Equality of laws gives \(\rho_k=\operatorname{laws}(P,U,\gamma,k)\). Relative entropy is a function of the two measures, so substitution transfers both the general normalized estimate and its \(N\alpha\) specialization. The initial law is also unchanged. Its divergence is measured against \(\Pi_N\), and normalization divides both initial and current joint entropy by \(N\).

The interpolation regularity assumptions remain assumptions on these same Euler laws. The equality of realizations adds no entropy estimate and requires no new analytic argument. The conclusions concern joint or projected probability-law divergence; concentration about a deterministic maximizing parameter is a separate assertion.

It is obtained by identifying its laws with particleLaws . gaussian_ipla_kl_bound_of_linear_lsi : The \(N\alpha\) lifted-LSI specialization for the actual Gaussian IPLA realization, with every algorithm-law assumption retained.

IPLA/LSI/Marginal.lean.title: Relative entropy under parameter projection
IPLA/LSI/Marginal.lean.summary: Project the current state law and the lifted Gibbs law by the same measurable parameter map. The data-processing inequality bounds the projected relative entropy by the joint relative entropy. A finite joint divergence makes the projected divergence finite and permits both to be read as real numbers. This argument needs neither a formula for the marginal density nor strong convexity or a distinguished maximizing parameter.

steps.title: The projected target as a probability measure
steps.body:
Put \(p=p_\theta\) and define \(\Pi_N^\theta=p_\#\Pi_N\). The continuous linear projection is measurable. For every probability measure \(\mu\),

\((p_\#\mu)(\mathbb R^{d_\theta})=\mu(p^{-1}(\mathbb R^{d_\theta}))=\mu(\mathbb R^D)=1\).

Thus it preserves probability, both for the current state law and for the reference whenever \(\Pi_N\) is normalized. In the conditional entropy result this normalization is part of the logarithmic Sobolev assumption. The definition \(\Pi_N^\theta=(p_\theta)_\#\Pi_N\) fixes the parameter reference as a measure even when no marginal-potential representation has been established.

Formal correspondence: parameterTarget : The parameter target is the actual lifted Gibbs law projected to its parameter coordinates. Probability normalization remains an explicit premise. parameterLaw_isProbability : Projecting a probability-valued state law preserves probability mass. parameterTarget_isProbability : The Gibbs parameter target is normalized whenever the actual joint target is normalized. No concentration or convexity hypothesis is introduced.

steps.title: Data processing for extended relative entropy
steps.body:
For a measurable projection the data-processing inequality states

\[\operatorname{KL}(p_\#\mu\Vert p_\# u)\le\operatorname{KL}(\mu\Vert u).\]

Convexity of \(u\log u\) implies that averaging over the discarded coordinates cannot increase divergence. The measure-theoretic theorem expresses this without requiring an explicit conditional density. Its inequality is meaningful in the extended nonnegative reals. If the joint divergence is finite, the inequality also makes the projected divergence finite; conversion of both finite quantities to real numbers then preserves order. This is the finite form used in the numerical bounds.

The parameter projection is a continuous linear map and hence measurable. Data processing gives the extended inequality \(\operatorname{KL}(p_\#\mu\Vert p_\# u)\le\operatorname{KL}(\mu\Vert u)\) before any real conversion. A finite joint KL therefore proves finite marginal KL, and only then can ENNReal.toReal_le_toReal transfer the order. This is a divergence statement about the actual pushed-forward target, with no density formula or optimizer concentration assumed.

Formal correspondence: parameter_kl_le_joint : Extended-valued data processing for the common parameter projection. parameter_kl_ne_top_of_joint : Finite joint KL implies finite parameter KL. parameter_klReal_le_joint : The real data-processing inequality, with finiteness of both divergences established before taking their toReal values.

steps.title: Full and per-particle entropy upper bounds
steps.body:
If the full finite joint divergence satisfies \(H\le B\), data processing bounds the parameter divergence by \(B\). If only \(H/N\le B\) is given with \(N>0\), multiplication gives \(H\le NB\), hence

\[\operatorname{KL}(p_\#\mu\Vert p_\#\nu)\le NB.\]

In particular the estimate \(H/N\le B\), multiplied by positive \(N\), becomes \(H\le NB\). Projection then gives upper bound \(NB\) rather than \(B\). With iteration notation \(H_k/N\le B_k\), the same operation gives \(H_k\le NB_k\) and therefore \(H_k^\theta\le NB_k\) rather than \(B_k\).

The initial quantity in the resulting parameter estimate is still the full initial joint entropy. Data processing makes the projected initial entropy smaller; it does not justify substituting that smaller number into an upper bound derived for the joint evolution. Both the normalization factor and the initial term must therefore be retained.

steps.title: The inequality for the Gibbs parameter projection
steps.body:
Set \(\nu=\Pi_N\) in the generic projection theorem. The definition of \(\Pi_N^\theta\) gives \(\operatorname{KL}(p_\#\mu\Vert\Pi_N^\theta)\le\operatorname{KL}(\mu\Vert\Pi_N)\). Joint finiteness implies projected finiteness, and any finite real joint upper bound therefore transfers to the parameter divergence.

Both laws are projected by the same map. Their normalization and the finite-joint condition are inherited from the joint theorem. This specialization requires no density regularity, particle independence, concentration estimate, or optimizer assumption beyond those used to establish that theorem.

IPLA/LSI/Corollaries.lean.title: Conditional parameter-entropy estimates
IPLA/LSI/Corollaries.lean.summary: The conditional joint entropy theorem and data processing give finite parameter divergence and its numerical estimate. The initial term is the full initial joint entropy, and an estimate normalized by particle count is multiplied by that count before it bounds the unnormalized parameter divergence.

steps.title: Finiteness of the parameter divergence
steps.body:
The Gaussian transition makes \(\rho_k\) a probability, and the logarithmic Sobolev assumption normalizes \(\Pi_N\). Under the interpolation assumptions, the finite joint entropy conclusion holds for \(\gamma\ge0\). Data processing therefore gives \(\operatorname{KL}(p_{\theta\#}\rho_k\Vert\Pi_N^\theta)<\infty\).

This conclusion is first an extended-valued finiteness statement. It establishes that the projected divergence is an ordinary finite number before a numerical upper bound is applied. No extra parameter-density formula is required.

Formal correspondence: parameter_kl_finite : Finite actual joint IPLA KL supplies finite actual parameter KL.

steps.title: The parameter estimate from the full joint bound
steps.body:
Assume \(N>0\), \(\beta>0\), \(\beta\le NL\), and \(0<\gamma\le\beta/(4NL^2)\), together with the conditional interpolation hypotheses. The joint theorem gives \(H_k\le e^{-\beta\gamma k/N}H_0+8\gamma ND L^2/\beta\). The joint divergence is finite, so data processing yields

\[\operatorname{KL}(p_{\theta\#}\rho_k\Vert\Pi_N^\theta)\le e^{-\beta\gamma k/N}H_0+\frac{8\gamma ND L^2}{\beta}.\]

Here \(H_0=\operatorname{KL}(\mu_0\Vert\Pi_N)\). At the same iteration \(k\), projection decreases only the divergence on the left; substitution of the joint bound leaves its initial quantity, exponential, and error term unchanged. The initial quantity includes parameter and latent information. The estimate compares parameter probability laws and does not itself give concentration about a likelihood maximizer.

Formal correspondence: parameter_kl_bound : The actual parameter marginal inherits the full joint KL bound for any supplied lifted LSI constant \(\beta\). The initial entropy is the full joint entropy.

steps.title: Parameter divergence under a linearly scaled lifted constant
steps.body:
Suppose the logarithmic Sobolev constant of the lifted target is \(N\alpha\). The conditional normalized theorem gives

\[\frac{H_k}{N}\le e^{-\alpha\gamma k}\frac{H_0}{N}+\frac{8\gamma L^2}{\alpha}\left(d_x+\frac{d_\theta}{N}\right).\]

To bound the unnormalized parameter divergence, multiply the complete upper bound by positive \(N\). Data processing gives upper bound

\[N\left[e^{-\alpha\gamma k}\frac{H_0}{N}+\frac{8\gamma L^2}{\alpha}\left(d_x+\frac{d_\theta}{N}\right)\right].\]

For constant \(N\alpha\) the multiplication by \(N\) is explicitly

\[\operatorname{KL}(p_\#\rho_k\Vert p_\#\Pi_N)\le N\left[e^{-\alpha\gamma k}\frac{H_0}{N}+\frac{8\gamma L^2}{\alpha}(d_x+d_\theta/N)\right].\]

Probability normalization and finite joint entropy justify the finite data-processing inequality. Multiplication by \(N\) restores the initial quantity \(H_0\) and gives error term \(8\gamma L^2D/\alpha\), exactly as direct substitution of \(\beta=N\alpha\) into the full estimate does. The interpolation and lifted logarithmic Sobolev hypotheses remain in force, and this conclusion concerns divergence between probability laws.

steps.title: The infimum over finite-cost initial couplings
steps.body:

Suppose its initial \(L^2\) discrepancy is bounded by \(\operatorname{cost}(c)\) and all realizations have the same numerical output law \(\mu_k\). steps.title: The projected root mean square inequality on a coupling
steps.body:
Let \(T\) be a linear contraction, \(b\) a fixed center, and \(c\) a coupling of \(\mu,\pi\). The decomposition \(Tx-b=T(x-y)+(Ty-b)\) and bound \(\|T(x-y)\|\le\|x-y\|\) imply

\[\|Tx-b\|_{L^2(\mu)}\le\operatorname{cost}(c)+\|Ty-b\|_{L^2(\pi)}.\]

Taking the infimum of the coupling cost replaces that term by \(W_2(\mu,\pi)\). Finiteness of transport and of the equilibrium radius first implies finiteness of the sampled projected second moment, whose real root mean square value is \(\sqrt{\int\|Tx-b\|^2d\mu}\).

Equivalently, for coupling variables \(X,Y\), the identity \(TX-b=T(X-Y)+(TY-b)\) and inequality \(\|T(X-Y)\|_2\le\|X-Y\|_2\) give the estimate by Minkowski. The marginal laws identify the first and equilibrium root mean square quantities, and the coupling cost bounds the remaining term. steps.title: The segment equation and common Euler innovations
steps.body:
On each interval \([kh,(k+1)h]\), solve the drift integral equation in \(L^2\) from the preceding terminal value:

\[Y_{k,t}-Y_{k,0}=-\int_0^t\nabla V(Y_{k,s})ds+\sqrt2\bigl(B_{kh+t}-B_{kh}\bigr).\]

Lipschitz continuity gives existence, uniqueness, and mean-square continuity, so adjacent segments agree at their common endpoint. The Brownian noise term at the endpoint, normalized by \(\sqrt{2h}\), gives the Euler innovation. Its second moment gives the interval noise bound \(\sqrt{2d}\sqrt t\).

If every reference-time law is the Gibbs law, the score-moment estimate gives \(\|\nabla V(Y_{k,t})\|_{L^2}\le\sqrt{Ld}\) uniformly over intervals. These integral, joining, noise, and drift bounds permit the same local comparison at every step. The segment construction alone does not prove the all-time Gibbs-law premise; that stationarity assertion is supplied independently.

steps.title: Independence of initialization and the noise source
steps.body:
Use probability space \((H\times H)\times S\) with measure \(c\otimes Q\). The two initial variables are the coordinates of \(c\), and the innovations depend only on \(S\). Product independence makes the initial pair independent of the noise. The first recursion applies \(x\mapsto x-h\nabla V(x)+\sqrt{2h}\xi_k\). Its output is the measurable pushforward of \(\mu_0\otimes Q\), so it depends on \(\mu_0\) and not on coupling \(c\). Finite coupling cost and the target second moment give the required \(L^2\) initial variables.

Writing the initial pair as \(X_0,Y_0\) and the noise coordinate as \(S\), under \(c\otimes Q\) the pair \((X_0,S)\) has law \(\mu_0\otimes Q\). The numerical recursion therefore has a fixed law across choices of the initial coupling. The reference starts at \(Y_0\) and uses the same noise, giving a synchronous comparison for each initial cost. A finite such comparison proves output finiteness before the transport infimum is converted to a real estimate.

IPLA/ProductBrownian.lean.title: Independent Brownian increments and Gaussian innovations
IPLA/ProductBrownian.lean.summary:
Independent Brownian coordinate paths on a probability space independent of the initial pair provide both the continuous reference noise and the Gaussian Euler innovations. Pullback to the product space preserves the Brownian distributions. Normalization of each increment gives unit Gaussian variance and retains independence across coordinates and disjoint time intervals.

The exported shared module pulls an independent Brownian coordinate source to the product of that source with an arbitrary initial coupling. IPLA adds only its state-coordinate adapter in ULAAdapter.lean.

steps.title: Brownian increments on the coupling product space
steps.body:
Projection from the coupling–noise product onto the noise coordinate preserves its probability law. Pulling each Brownian coordinate back by this projection therefore preserves its Brownian law. Define

\[\xi_{k,a}=\frac{B_a((k+1)h)-B_a(kh)}{\sqrt h},\qquad h>0.\]

Independent increments and independent coordinate paths give mutual independence over \(k\) and \(a\). The product measure makes the entire noise sequence independent of both initial coordinates.

A scalar increment over an interval of length \(h\) has centered Gaussian law with variance \(h\), and division by \(\sqrt h\) makes it standard Gaussian. Its square integrability also follows from this variance. The normalized noise is the same increment used in the reference integral equation. The product gives the prescribed Gibbs initial coordinate; all-time stationarity remains a separate premise at this intermediate stage and is proved in the complete diffusion construction.

IPLA.lean.title: Interacting particle Langevin: transport and entropy convergence
IPLA.lean.summary:
The same Gaussian interacting-particle recursion admits two kinds of estimates. Joint strong convexity gives a quadratic-transport bound and parameter root mean square error about a marginal-likelihood maximizer. A logarithmic Sobolev inequality for the coupled particle target gives relative-entropy bounds for the joint and projected laws. The hypotheses, initial quantities, and particle normalizations differ and are stated separately.

The root module imports the complete particle library. It exports the strongly convex transport/RMS theorem together with the separate conditional lifted-LSI entropy route. It adds no declarations of its own; the linked dependency modules provide the detailed mathematical and Lean proofs.

steps.title: The strongly convex transport and parameter estimates
steps.body:
In scaled coordinates the summed potential has explicit curvature and gradient constants. These regularity properties normalize its Gibbs law and permit a stationary Langevin coupling for the full-state transport bound. Latent integration independently identifies the parameter Gibbs marginal and proves its concentration about the unique marginal-likelihood maximizer. Projection and Minkowski’s inequality then add equilibrium concentration to the transport estimate, giving the equilibrium, transient, and discretization terms in the parameter bound.

The imported chain begins with \(V_N(\theta,z)=\sum_iU(\theta,\sqrt Nz_i)\), proves dimension \(d_\theta+Nd_x\), convexity \(Nm\) and smoothness \(NL\), identifies the Gaussian algorithm with step \(\gamma/N\), and applies shared Gaussian ULA transport. In parallel, Gaussian domination and proved Prékopa–Leindler identify the parameter target and prove its \(Nm\)-strong convexity. The final projection estimate adds equilibrium radius \(\sqrt{2d_\theta/(Nm)}\), transient transport \((1-m\gamma)^kW_2(\mu_0,\Pi_N)\), and Euler bias \((33/20)(L/m)\sqrt{d_x+d_\theta/N}\sqrt\gamma\). Root import therefore exposes a theorem whose normalization, moments, stationarity and concentration inputs have all been derived.

steps.title: The joint and parameter entropy estimates
steps.body:
The entropy estimate concerns the relative entropy of the current joint law with respect to the lifted Gibbs target. Applying data processing to both laws gives the projected parameter-law divergence. It does not by itself give concentration about a deterministic maximizing parameter. The conditional interpolation theorem and the Gaussian interpolation construction establish their respective entropy estimates under the distinct assumptions stated in each result.

The LSI imports instead assume an LSI of constant \(\beta\) for the actual \(\Pi_N\) and the regular interpolation data needed by the shared entropy proof. They prove finite actual KL and \(H_k\le e^{-\beta\gamma k/N}H_0+8\gamma N(d_\theta+Nd_x)L^2/\beta\), then derive normalized and parameter-projection consequences. The \(\beta=N\alpha\) specialization is explicitly additional. Run lake build IPLA and the two audit modules to check the public endpoints and their dependency chains.

IPLA/LSI/UnconditionalTheorem.lean.title: Particle-entropy convergence from the lifted logarithmic Sobolev inequality
IPLA/LSI/UnconditionalTheorem.lean.summary: The Gaussian interpolation theorem derives the required density, differentiation, and integrability properties from the entropy assumptions. For the particle model, substitute \(V_N\), step \(\gamma/N\), gradient constant \(NL\), and dimension \(D=d_\theta+Nd_x\). The lifted-target logarithmic Sobolev inequality, positive admissible step, and finite initial joint entropy then imply finite output entropy and the quantitative estimate. Division by particle count and parameter projection give the stated corollaries.

steps.title: Finite joint entropy and its convergence estimate
steps.body:
Let \(N>0\), \(D=d_\theta+Nd_x\), and \(V_N(z)=\sum_iU(\theta,\sqrt N z_i)\). Assume differentiability of \(U\) with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, a logarithmic Sobolev inequality of constant \(\beta>0\) for \(\Pi_N\), a positive physical step satisfying \(\gamma\le\beta/(4NL^2)\), and finite initial joint entropy \(H_0\). Every particle law then has finite divergence and satisfies

\[H_k\le e^{-\beta\gamma k/N}H_0+\frac{8\gamma ND L^2}{\beta}.\]

The lifted potential is differentiable with \(NL\)-Lipschitz gradient, and its Gaussian Euler law at step \(h=\gamma/N\) is the particle law. The physical restriction is equivalent to \(h\le\beta/(4(NL)^2)\). Thus the Gaussian interpolation theorem applies with \(h=\gamma/N\), dimension \(D\), and gradient constant \(NL\). Its rate is \(e^{-\beta\gamma k/N}\) and its error is \(8\gamma ND L^2/\beta\). The admissible positive step also gives positive \(L\) before any division.

In detail, the squared gradient constant is \(\ell^2=N^2L^2\) and the step is \(h=\gamma/N\). These substitutions give restriction \(\gamma\le\beta/(4NL^2)\) and error term \(8\gamma NDL^2/\beta\). The Gaussian theorem supplies the interpolation regularity and the compatibility of constants, so neither is an additional premise here. The finite-divergence conclusion is retained alongside the real inequality, justifying each real-valued entropy in the formula.

steps.title: The entropy bound divided by particle count
steps.body:
Divide the finite joint entropy inequality by positive \(N\). Division preserves order and gives

\[\frac{H_k}{N}\le e^{-\beta\gamma k/N}\frac{H_0}{N}+\frac{8\gamma D L^2}{\beta}.\]

Because \(N>0\), every term is divided by the same finite positive number. The exponential is unchanged, and its initial factor is the initial joint entropy per particle. This is a numerical normalization of the joint divergence, not the divergence of the parameter marginal.

The helper normalize_entropy_bound divides both the initial contribution and the bias, canceling one particle factor in the latter. The same finite-KL witness is retained for the unnormalized divergence. This quantity is the entropy of the full state divided by particle number; parameter projection is handled separately.

steps.title: A linearly scaled lifted logarithmic Sobolev constant
steps.body:
Assume the lifted Gibbs target has logarithmic Sobolev constant \(\beta=N\alpha\) with \(\alpha>0\). Positivity of particle count gives \(\beta>0\), and the restriction \(\gamma\le\beta/(4NL^2)\) becomes \(\gamma\le\alpha/(4L^2)\). Apply the normalized joint theorem with this constant. Its rate is \(e^{-\alpha\gamma k}\). The dimension equality \(D/N=d_x+d_\theta/N\) gives error term \((8\gamma L^2/\alpha)(d_x+d_\theta/N)\), so

\[\frac{H_k}{N}\le e^{-\alpha\gamma k}\frac{H_0}{N}+\frac{8\gamma L^2}{\alpha}\left(d_x+\frac{d_\theta}{N}\right).\]

The functional-inequality premise concerns \(\Pi_N\) itself. The relation \(D/N=d_x+d_\theta/N\) separates the intensive latent and parameter contributions. Since the particles share a parameter, no product tensorization of independent pair targets is used to obtain the assumed constant.

steps.title: The parameter-entropy consequence
steps.body:
Project both the particle law and its Gibbs reference to their parameter coordinates. Data processing gives \(\operatorname{KL}(\mu_k^\theta\Vert\Pi_N^\theta)\le H_k\). The joint theorem supplies \(H_k<\infty\), so the projected divergence is finite as well. Substitution of the full numerical estimate yields

\[\operatorname{KL}(\mu_k^\theta\Vert\Pi_N^\theta)\le e^{-\beta\gamma k/N}H_0+\frac{8\gamma ND L^2}{\beta}.\]

The initial quantity is the full joint entropy \(H_0\). The parameter divergence is unnormalized, so its error retains factor \(N\). If a joint bound is supplied per particle, it must first be multiplied by \(N\). Data processing changes only the left-hand divergence and does not replace the initial joint entropy by a smaller projected quantity.
